speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley) moved:
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to protect Canadian interests regarding the interbasin transfer of water as exemplified by the Kemano project, the North Thompson River, and both the Columbia River Tteaty and the North American free trade agreement.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased and honoured to present this motion on a very important issue to the people of northern British Columbia and the entire country. It concerns what many would perhaps say is our life-blood. That is our water and in particular our rivers in northern British Columbia, in my constituency, the Nechako River, the North Thompson River and other river systems.
Before putting some comments on the record I would like to first thank my colleagues for their support in bringing this very important motion forward.
I want to comment today on the ongoing Kemano controversy in northern British Columbia. The arguments I intend to make today are of the complicity of this government in hiding information on this matter.
I want to thank my colleagues from what we call the caucus for interior British Columbia. They are members from the interior of B.C. who have concerns about issues outside the island and lower mainland of B.C. They are
There are two water diversion issues in my constituency that I would like to speak on today. One is in the western end of my riding and is known to this House as the Kemano controversy. The other is at the eastern end and is a developing project called the North Thompson diversion, which is currently being promoted by a gentleman named Mr. Clancy from the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I want to speak primarily on the concerns that I and the vast majority of my constituents and others in British Columbia have over the Kemano issue and its potential impact on the Nechako River.
I would like to give a brief history of the situation we have got into, to outline some of the concerns that people have in northern B.C. and to review what has been done to date but particularly to review what has not been done by this government.
The Kemano controversy is a megaproject in northern B.C. I will not go into all of the history on this. Much has been written and much more will be written about this particular project.
In short, a project in the late 1950s developed the community of Kitimat. The massive Nechako reservoir was created around Ootsa Lake for electrical power at Kemano which was transmitted to Kitimat for the production of aluminum. That project continued for some time as part of the arrangement that was signed between the then provincial government with the acquiescence of the then federal government.
There was always the prospect that the company would proceed with another part of its project, Kemano II. It is

May 28, 1993
Supply
that debate and the current history on that project that I would like to focus my comments on today.
It is remarkable and revealing in this issue of just how we mismanage our water resources. If there is a list of projects that we should learn from as to how not to manage our resources, the Kemano project would be one, the W.A.C. Bennett dam would be another, and there have been a host of other projects across this country. If there is any lesson that we can learn at all, that is not the way to proceed when it comes to these kinds of projects.
In the current history there was the struggle by the federal government at the time to have the right to manage the Nechako River. In fact, the government of the day won that particular fight against the Alcan company. The company wanted to reduce the flows in that river so that it would have more water in its reservoir to pipe through to its hydroelectric generating plant.
It was revealing that after the federal government won an injunction it had the right on behalf of all Canadians to manage the affairs of that river and the company, a multinational corporation, decided to challenge that injunction. That set in motion a string of events we in northern B.C. are now paying the price for.
What we have learned from the few documents that have seen the light of day on this project is that as the federal government was preparing to defend the right to control and manage that river, a backroom deal was signed. This government arranged to settle out of court and in 1987 the Nechako settlement agreement was reached. It is that settlement agreement upon which much of the debate currently revolves.
Some of the concerns that existed prior to the settlement agreement and that exist to this day about the Nechako River are summed up well by a headline in the Prince George Citizen on June 1, 1990. An article about Kemano called "Inside a megaproject" said: "You will wonder where the water went".
That is what the people of northern British Columbia will be asking. They will be asking about the flows in the Nechako River. They will be asking about its impact on
migrating salmon. They will be asking about water intakes and outlets for some of the communities along that river. They will be asking about its impact on wildlife and they will be asking about its impact on agriculture and irrigation.
In other words, there are a host of concerns on this particular river alone. The people of northern B.C. have been calling for a full public review for a chance to present their views in an official forum and to hear and see the information that both governments and in particular the proponent, the Alcan aluminium company, have on this project.
What we have learned from documents that have been released is that this Government of Canada has already said through its access to information officers that it has some 83,000 pages of information on this project. Now it says it is only prepared to release a limited number of those documents to the public so that it can see what is happening on this project.
If this project can stand on its own two feet and if this government says that everything is okay then why does it refuse to release those documents?
From the evidence that has seen the light of day so far on this project we have learned why this government refuses to release information on this project. The memos and documents that I have obtained and have released to the public indicate on the one hand that at one point there was an effort to try to develop a federal-provincial review. However for some reason this did not happen, and I suggest that reason is in the filing cabinet of the current Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the previous Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the current Minister of Forestry. The reasons for hiding this information exist in their filing cabinets.
We have gathered further information from documents released from within the department. This one in particular is dated December 11, 1987 and is by a consultant who reviewed the information on this particular project. It is directed to the deputy minister for fisheries and oceans. It says: "I am worried about these words. They create the impression that the agreement has numerous negative implications". He would like to see that corrected. It continues: "It looks like an inquiry, the exact thing that this government has refused to conduct and refuses to participate in".
May 28, 1993

People in northern B.C. have called for the federal government and the former provincial government to conduct a full review of this project. It was an issue, and I have some scars from it.
In the 1984 election, which was the election prior to the Nechako settlement agreement of 1987, the government of the day, now the Official Opposition, could have told Canadians where it stood on this issue. Where does it stand? The Conservative Party was opposed to a public review. It was opposed to releasing information. It was opposed to providing funds to chambers of commerce, community groups and environmental groups to get to the bottom of this project before it went ahead.
Who supported the Conservatives? The Official Opposition, the Liberal Party, was opposed to a full public review and opposed to the release of information. The Liberals and Conservatives worked together at those all-candidate forums to deny the people of northern B.C. an opportunity to have the truth come out about this project. They are tied together in this. The complicity of the Liberals, the Conservatives and the Social Credit government of the day has denied the people of northern B.C. an opportunity to have a full say and full information on this particular project.
It has only been through the election of a new government in British Columbia that we are finally being given an opportunity to have some say in this project. That is being done by the announcement by the premier of British Columbia and the minister of the environment, the Hon. John Cashore, of a public review under the utilities commission to look into this project and its impact on the Nechako River. If the terms of reference are refined as I hope they are we will learn its possible impact on the Fraser River as well.
Some people were disappointed that the government did not feel it was able to use its legislative power to block the project entirely. Some of my constituents wished that the government had done that. I will tell you, Madam Speaker, about the kind of corporate blackmail we are dealing with on this project. Headlines from the Alcan aluminum company at limited shareholder meetings: "Alcan threatens to sue government" "Al-
Supply
can threatens to sue if they don't get then way", a way paid for them by Socreds and Conservatives.
We now have a review. We are urging all people in northern B.C. to participate and present their views about this project. I presented my submission to the commission and outlined what I thought concerning its procedural matters and the issues it should take a look at.
I suggested full public meetings throughout northern B.C. and the communities of Bums Lake, Fraser Lake, Fort Fraser, Vanderhoof, Fort St. James, Prince George, as well as communities outside that area that are affected by this project.
I suggested that the utilities commission use its authority and its powers of subpoena if the federal government in particular was not willing voluntarily to provide all of the information on this project. The commission should use its subpoena powers and compel evidence and compel witnesses to attend those hearings.
We have only just learned from a letter dated April 30, 1993 from the Department of Justice to the utilities commission of the federal government's official view of its participation in this inquiry. It is the one that we expected, the limited release of information. This is revealing because it goes to the heart of this government's attempts to avoid dealing with the truth of this matter.
A paragraph in the letter suggests-and this is where it may all end up-that the government will not participate in even the limited release of information as a waiver by the federal government of its right to object to the authority of the commission to obtain disclosure of information or to subpoena past or present federal government employees in order to elicit information obtained by them in the course of their duties.
We know what that means. This government will use its clout to stop the ongoing attempts to get to the truth of this matter. It is all said here and as my colleague says it is a gag order. That is exactly what it is and that is what we face from this government.
We could go on for days talking about the concerns that the people of northern B.C. have about this project. We have enumerated them in election campaigns. We have enumerated them in committee meetings, in public

May 28, 1993
Supply
meetings and in this Chamber as well. Still this government refuses to listen to the people of northern B.C.
I use this platform and this opportunity to encourage my constituents, the people of British Columbia to participate in that public inquiry.
I urge Alcan to participate in the inquiry. The day the provincial government announced this review Alcan condemned it. Shame on Alcan for that. But it did leave the door open for possible participation in the future.
Alcan owes it to the people of northern British Columbia for the millions and millions of dollars it has made from the people of British Columbia so far to date and the millions and millions of dollars it might make. It owes it to the people of northern B.C. to appear before that commission and to present its side of the argument.
Shame on it for not participating to date. It has the rights and the responsibilities of any other intervener to participate in that inquiry. I ask Alcan to tell the people of northern B.C. why it refuses to participate. I ask the Government of Canada to tell the people of northern B.C. why it refuses to release information and to become a full partner in the review of this project.
The evidence continues to mount about the concerns that people have all across this country now, the concerns of the Cheslatta, the concerns of the people of Fort Fraser who I think have earned the credit of northern B.C. for the work they have done on this project, for the people in Vanderhoof who have been struggling on this issue, for the Allied Rivers Commission in Prince George, and all the people who are taking petitions around and attending public meetings.
Even in these hallowed chambers we have headlines coming in now: "Parliamentary committee reports Ke-mano decision termed illegal." I know that we will hear more about this particular matter in the weeks to come.
It is because we take our concerns about our water, and in particular our rivers, seriously whether it is a goofy proposal by somebody in Vancouver to divert the North Thompson River into Kinbasket Lake and to sell
the water to the United States, or it is a cover-up by the federal government of an issue concerning the Nechako and the Kemano controversy. It is no wonder people are concerned. Water is our life-blood and it has been mismanaged and mistreated by this government and governments preceding it. The people of British Columbia ask. What is going on?
I will leave the last words to the people of Prince George-Bulkley Valley as to how they feel about this issue. I want to quote from a letter that the president of the Allied Rivers Commission sent to two of the leadership contenders in the Conservative Party's leadership race. It concerns the news this week of the illegality of the government's position on this matter. I quote:
As members of cabinet, I hold you both accountable for
deliberately undermining the integrity of our parliamentary
democracy.
Who was in the cabinet room when they made every effort to avoid sending this project to a full environmental review? We want to know. The people of northern B.C. want to know which cabinet ministers were there who are willing to allow a river to disappear.
Let me just read a couple of comments in the short time I have left from replies to the surveys I have conducted. From Fort Fraser, B.C.: "I would like Alcan to explain to the people of this province where the 30,000 to 40,000 jobs are that they promised to create after completion of the Kemano I project. Don't sell our river. Its value is much greater than we can imagine".
This from Fort Fraser again: "Alcan failed to build the 40,000 to 50,000 job industrial complex. They are not living up to the agreement". There is a rude comment about the president of Alcan.
I have hundreds and hundreds of these kinds of comments that the people of my constituency of northern B.C. and all of British Columbia are saying about our rivers, in particular the Nechako and the North Thompson Rivers.
I implore the government to join now with the province of B.C. to conduct a full joint review of this project. Release all of the information that is available and give our rivers a chance.
May 28, 1993

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, in presenting a case that is a concern not only to his constituents but to all of British Columbia.
I would like to direct a question to my colleague. Some time back in this Chamber when I was speaking on water exports, one of the members on the government side said, as close as I can recall the phrase, that the Americans are not interested in Canadian water, there is no interest by the Americans to import Canadian waters either into California or other parts of the United States or down into Mexico. I said at the time that the member either had simply lost track 5f reality or was completely unaware of developments over the past couple of decades.
There is a proposal that is in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, that is on the books now, a serious proposal with big money backing. That is a proposal to divert a portion of the flow of the North Thompson River at Valemount, British Columbia, to tunnel right through a mountain side and actually divert that water, one-third of the flow of the North Thompson River, into a large reservoir that is part of the Columbia River system at this point and then to divert that one million acre feet a year through the Columbia system, down into the California market.
I would like to ask the member what kind of impact the diversion of one-third of the flow of the North Thompson River would have on the salmon migration, the effect upon the entire flow of the Fraser River system and the imbalance of the whole watershed in the Thompson-Fraser system, what will be the environmental impact and whether or not this proposal is truly a serious proposal because there is some question whether these kinds of proposals can fly.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the member's question. He is very correct that there is a project currently being promoted in British Columbia to divert part of the North Thompson River into what is called Kinbasket Lake just south of the community of Vale-mount. Kinbasket Lake forms the top end, the northern end of the entire Columbia River Treaty system and the impact is shared not just in my constituency but also that of our colleague, the member for Kamloops. We have

held a number of public meetings on this matter both in Valemount and recently in Kamloops.
For the seriousness of the proposal I suppose we can read some of the comments from the promoter. The promoter's name is Mr. Clancy who hails from the lower mainland of British Columbia where he has clearly obtained some funding from somebody to finance this proposal.
I will read a quote from the August 24, 1992 issue of Maclean's magazine. This kind of sums up the approach that Mr. Clancy and his company is taking. I am quoting Mr. Clancy: "If it does not happen the United States will come and take it", he said, "They've got to have water and it will be more valuable than oil".
I think that probably says it all. Mr. Clancy is currently writing construction unions across the province asking them to endorse his proposal. We thank the building trades union representative who got up at the interior MPs' meeting in Kamloops to say: "Just hold it a minute". The construction unions are not going to rush to Mr. Clancy's support in order to get the few shortterm jobs that would come from this project. We congratulate the trade union movement for their support of our cause on this matter.
The point the member is making about the cumulative effect of the impact of this project, of the Kemano controversy and its impact on the Nechako River, the cumulative effect on the Fraser River, which on the other hand we are trying to protect and bring back to good health, is a very good one.
On the one hand the federal government prides itself on its Fraser River action plan and, on the other hand, what is it doing with the Nechako and with the North Thompson? It is going to destroy the Fraser River as well.
The point was well made by a former fisheries and oceans scientist who is volunteering with the Cheslatta Indian band, saying it dramatically affected the rivers when the Alcan proposal went ahead. He talked about the cumulative effect on river systems that we might not always see. It is a project here, a project there. With the Tories it is a cover-up here and another cover-up over there. This will affect the flows in the Fraser River and it will obviously affect migrating salmon. That will happen

May 28, 1993

on the Fraser, up the North Thompson and throughout the entire watershed.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member has given a very wide-ranging account of the damage that would be done by the Kemano project and of the unwillingness of the federal government to co-operate in the most elementary way by providing information. He has referred also to the situation of some of the bands of Canada's native people there.
I wonder if he could enlarge a little bit on what is likely to be the effect generally on the bands of native people and what has been their response in the matter.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the member's question.
A lot of information could be provided on this matter. Briefly, the people that I feel for the most, and I hope others do who have seen some of the videos and information on this, are the Cheslatta people whose graveyards were flooded and whose village was burned to the ground by Alcan and by the Department of Indian Affairs. It is a tragic black mark on the history of native people in northern B.C. They have been diligent in attempting to get the information out about this project, using every opportunity that they have.
The invention of the fax machine has been a great aid in telling the world about their concerns. The Cheslatta people have presented to the utilities commission review their interest in what that review should do. They have compiled vast amounts of information on this project, as have a number of the other bands throughout the area. The Carrier-Sekani Tribal Council was part of some of the legal action, which I did not have time to go into today in my speech, against this government in attempting to get a full environmental review.
The Carrier people and in particular the Cheslatta and the people in Stony Creek, Nautley, all throughout that area have been following this issue. It directly affects their lives. For the government of the day to not listen and to turn a blind eye to those people is reason enough to open up the books and files so we can get to the truth of this matter. This will go a long way to rectify what has turned out to be a very black day in the history of northern B.C.

Madam Speaker, first let me express my appreciation to the Minister of State for the Environment for allowing me to speak ahead of her when it would normally be the government's prerogative to respond first. I do appreciate the courtesy, since it makes my life a little easier today.
I want to be a little less courteous to the member who has just spoken, however, and I do reserve the right to review the "blues" with respect to his comments earlier this week about the Liberal members of this Parliament, particularly in light of the specific statement of his colleague, the member for Skeena, on a matter that was not true. He said the Liberals were going to vote for NAFTA this week when he was in a position to know that was not the case.
Having had it proved to him this week I would like to have seen him pay the House the courtesy of withdrawing a wrong statement. However he has not done that.

Madam Speaker, on a point of order I do not want to drag this point out but I made no such reference one way or the other about how the Liberals were voting on the North American free trade agreement.
Nobody knows their position. How could you guess it?
My colleagues rightfully say they do not know their position.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of this motion and to condemn this government's negligence, abuse and failure to preserve and protect our most precious resource, water.
Water is essential to life. Ninety-eight per cent of the human body is water. Without it we and every living species on earth die. Without water, crops do not grow, forests do not flourish, soils become arid, sick and useless.

May 28, 1993

Our economic as well as our physical health depend on water. Water is essential to processing goods, keeping manufacturing equipment operating and transporting the commerce of the nation, the continent and the world. However water is more than an economic good. Water is the life-blood of the planet and of all ecological systems.
An eminent scientist said:
A river is more than a stream flowing through a valley to the ocean. It is part of one integral unit which begins at the heights of the land surrounding it and often continues far out to sea. Water unifies everything in the watershed falling as rain or snow, carving the land, circulating through the soil, the vegetation and every living thing including man.
The cycle is completed by rivers of water funnelled back into the atmosphere through trees and other vegetation and by water flowing to the sea from which currents of air carry moisture back to the highlands to fall again as rain and snow. The cycle continues eternally.
As the last century of industrial misuse, abuse and waste of water begins to reveal the toll it has taken on this most precious of resources, the quest for water threatens the security of nations and the globe.
I want to refer to the words of a former minister of the environment for the province of Quebec. When briefing a group of parliamentarians, he said:
As oil, diamonds, minerals were the precious resources of this century and the last century, the precious resource of the next century will be water.
In that context I want to examine the government's stewardship of this most precious of resources. I want to start with the free trade agreement and concentrate on that and the Kemano project. I want to leave other elements of the motion to speakers who will follow me.
I want to take us all back to the summer of 1988 which was certainly in my lifetime and the lifetime of most of us in this Parliament the hottest, driest summer we had ever experienced.
The debate about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was also hot as the government tried to delay an election until it could force the deal through Parliament. Only the clear message from the Liberal majority in the Senate that it would not pass the free trade agreement without an election sent this government to the polls. It
Supply
sent back a clear message that over 50 per cent of the Canadian voters did not support its position.
Water was the key element, perhaps because of the hot dry summer. Perhaps it was the rising concern of Canadians and people around the world for the devastation we were doing to our world that made them focus on what the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement states about water, and to conclude in large numbers that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement endangered Canada's natural water systems and endangered, if it did not destroy completely, our ability to protect that which Canadians find so precious.
The diversion of water is not a simple little tinkering with a bit of the geography of the world. This country has gone further than any other country in the world in rearranging the aquatic landscape. We have more diversions than any other country in the world. We have more than the United States with its 260 million people, more than China and more than the former U.S.S.R.
It is no wonder Canadians were worried about what the free trade agreement would do to our ability to decide whether we would or would not continue to rearrange the map of the planet to suit our own needs and the economic demands of others.
The government has continued to maintain that water is not covered in the free trade agreement so I want to just put on the record a few arguments that say it is. These arguments were made about the free trade agreement in 1988 and they still hold with respect to the NAFTA in 1993.
I do not think Canadians need to be reminded of the disgraceful travesty of Parliament that has taken place this week with the ramming through of the North American free trade agreement with barely three days of debate. The government forced the opposition to defend the public interest by debating around the clock. Even then we only barely touched on the essential and crucial elements in that agreement in public debate.
I want to go straight to the NAFTA because the government was asked during the free trade agreement to try to protect our waters and it did not do that. It was

May 28, 1993
Supply
asked again when it was negotiating NAFTA to try to protect our waters and it did not do that.
I want to go to tariff heading 2201 of the NAFTA which defines water and includes natural or artificial and mineral waters and aerated waters not containing added sugar or other sweetening matter nor flavoured; in other words natural water, ice and snow.
We can go to other sections but I will quote an opinion given to Mr. Don Gamble, the former executive director of the Rawson Academy by a lawyer who had advised the federal government in the water trade debate in 1988. He stated: "In conclusion it is my opinion that any water, other than sea water, would be classifiable under tariff item 2201 regardless of the quantity of water imported and regardless of its use".
The government has consistently argued that is not the case. It has attempted to put a proviso in the legislation as it did in 1988 with the free trade agreement saying that for greater certainty nothing in this act or the agreement except article 302 of the agreement applies to water.
However, one party to an agreement cannot unilaterally decide what the terms of that agreement mean. The government knows that perfectly well and so do the United States and Mexican governments.
We can quibble about one legal interpretation of the free trade agreement and NAFTA or another. The fact is that if the government was serious about exempting water from the free trade agreement it had the opportunity when it negotiated NAFTA to have its trading partners agree to include that in the agreement. If it believes that to be the case there would have been no problem having it included in the agreement. One has to be suspicious as to why it was not done.
One has to be even more suspicious as we now renegotiate around environmental issues with the new administration in the United States. Why is our government so anxious not to have a strong agreement on the environment, given the assurances it has given Canadians and the position it has tried to defend? Why with the negotiations reopened is it not including this issue which is of such great concern to Canadians in those negotiations and insisting on it in the agreement or in a parallel agreement?
Only a specific exclusion in NAFTA can truly give Canadians the assurance that they will not be forced and coerced under other terms of the agreement to divert water outside of this country to serve continental needs.
Lest anybody question whether water in rivers and lakes can be considered a good, let me draw the attention of Parliament and Canadians to Canada's participation at the international conference on water and the environment held in 1992. The conference noted that only by accepting that water is a tradable commodity like coal, oil and timber will sensible decisions be possible.
Canada, along with 99 other countries, adopted a statement from this international conference on water and the environment that has as its basic principle that water has an economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognized as an economic good. It is clearly subject to the terms and conditions of NAFTA including providing water to other countries even in times of shortage in Canada.
Our government in this case has perhaps most seriously jeopardized not only our control in this generation but the ability of future generations to determine how Canada's water will be used and whether we will continue the mass re-engineering of the continent that we have started with so many projects.
In the pitifully short debate that took place in the House this week, these issues could not be explored fully nor could they be in the couple of weeks allowed by the government for committee work. This is one of many serious issues that was irresponsibly not resolved. The government and the government alone is responsible for that.
I want to speak briefly about the Kemano project. My colleague from the NDP has spoken about the details of this project and its serious effects on aboriginal peoples, the salmon fishery, major rivers and a whole major river system. We simply cannot keep destroying ecological systems without knowing the impact on climate, soils, forests and the transmission of species that are harmful to the environment and yet this government has.
I want to briefly review a couple of points about the Kemano completion project. Plans to do the second phase of the Kemano project came forward in 1979. Alcan planned to totally and completely divert an entire
May 28, 1993

river. What was the response of the government of the day?
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in a Liberal government issued a ministerial order under the Fisheries Act requiring Alcan to increase water flows into the Nechako River to protect the fishery. Alcan refused to comply. The minister went to court and got an injunction and that injunction continued until October 1984.
In August 1984 before the 1984 general election the Liberal minister of fisheries, Romeo LeBlanc, responded to Alcan going to court against the injunction that had protected our fisheries and that river and said he would support a full public hearing into the Kemano completion project. What follows that is disgraceful.
Following the election of the Conservative government, in 1985 Alcan went to court to get rid of the injunction that the minister of fisheries had kept in place for over half a decade protecting the river.
This federal Tory government reached an agreement with Alcan to pave the way for the Kemano completion project. It was then challenged in court by environmental groups. Rather than responding to the environmental concerns by ordering an environmental assessment as it then had the authority to do, the federal government, knowing the environmental impacts of this project, specifically exempted Alcan from the Environmental Assessment Act and the requirement for a public environmental hearing.
It did more than that. It suppressed reports out of its own department. I was challenged by members on the other side when I said that in 1988 the government had suppressed information about the impacts of the free trade agreement and that it had reports from its own officials changed.
There is no doubt in this case that there are 83,000 pages of Department of Fisheries and Oceans documents relating to this project which have not been made publicly available so the public can see how this government is exercising its stewardship on behalf of our water.
I do not have a lot of time left but if we look at the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, there has been
very little process in protecting our Great Lakes which contain 20 per cent of the world's freshwater supply.
The same minister of fisheries who came to this tragic agreement with Alcan on the Kemano project is also the same later Minister of the Environment who exempted the Rafferty-Alameda Dam from the environmental assessment review process.
This government has consistently ignored decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada with regard to its environmental assessment responsibilities on the Oldman River Dam and the Rafferty-Alameda Dam. It has not yet responded to the report of its own environmental assessment review panel on the Oldman River Dam.
This country is fortunate enough to possess and control a disproportionate share of the world's geography and much of it is still in very good shape. That gives us an obligation, not only to our citizens and future generations of Canadians but to the world to protect that precious resource of which we have been given custody.
When it comes to water and the impacts of our preservation of water on all other natural systems this government has failed to do its duty. That is why we rise in support of this motion today.

Madam Speaker, it has now been three years since a fair election was held in Burma, which the military regime wants us to call Myanmar, and the National League for Democracy won a large majority.
One of the elected MPs, Aung San Suu Kyi, is a Nobel peace prize winner. She remains under house arrest and the military continues to rule by fear, forced labour, torture and rape.
The United Nations General Assembly and its human rights commission have repeatedly called for the regime to stop its abuses and move toward democracy.
Should thoughtful people not boycott companies such as Pepsi, Hostess and others that have operations in Burma and ties with the SLORC? Should Burma not be suspended from the UN until democracy is established?

Madam Speaker, yesterday the government used its majority to pass the North American free trade agreement in the House of Commons. Now it is up to the people of Canada to stop NAFTA.
May 28, 1993

In the next federal election Canadians will have a choice. If they want the free trade agreement and NAFTA they can vote for the Conservatives. If they believe that the free trade agreement and NAFTA must be stopped they know that the New Democratic Party will not allow these fundamentally flawed agreements to continue. If they want confusion they can support the Liberals who will not promise to kill the free trade agreement, who will not promise to stop NAFTA if there are no changes and who, even if they achieve their five desired changes to NAFTA, would still be supporting the sell-out of Canada.
The Liberal leader wants it both ways, he wants the financial support of big business and the votes of ordinary Canadians. However he cannot have it both ways. Madam Speaker, last Saturday people in the Northwest Territories and northern Alberta lost a well-known bush pilot in a tragic airplane accident.
Billy Bourque was 44 years old and was a very special Canadian. He was one of a handful of northern bush pilots with almost 10,000 flying hours. He deeply loved flying northerners to their trap lines and outpost camps. He made every effort to see that people in the bush were well taken care of.
Billy was also a passionate naturalist. He was an important contributor, helping to save the whooping cranes in Wood Buffalo National Park. He also worked over the years to catch poachers and fight fires.
Friends say he was the "bush pilot who was most at home making his plane dance through the trees and over the northern marshes".
Billy's sense of responsibility and contributions to the north brought him legendary fame and much respect. He will be sadly missed by all who loved, respected and knew him.

May 28, 1993

The hon. member has asked for a UN mission. I would be just as happy if the OAS sent one. Let me say this while I am on my feet. I want to reassure Canadians that our embassy has been in touch with every Canadian NGO group in Guatemala. All of them are all right, at least for the moment. The embassy has assisted those who want to leave to do so. Two left this morning. Some will be leaving this weekend. Others have expressed a preference to stay. The human rights conference participants have left or are leaving today.
Oral Questions
It is very important that we reassure Canadians that we do take action when we know that Canadians are at risk under this kind of political circumstance.

The province of Manitoba won a $6 million judgment against this person on April 17,1993 and the taxpayers of Canada are responsible for up to that amount through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The government chose to appoint him to the board of directors of the Bank of Canada 16 days after the judgment was rendered.
Why did the Deputy Prime Minister not know of this and why did he and his government appoint this person anyway? Why did they do it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:

Since it has been three days, what steps are being taken by the Government of Canada to recover these 200,000 taxpayer dollars improperly used to subsidize the leadership campaign of the Minister of the Environment?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that the hon. member's allegations are incorrect and I think present quite an unfair aspiration on the work of Mr. David Small.
As I indicated in the House earlier this week, Mr. Small was selected by the Department of the Environment to provide very critical communications advice and planning for the UNCED conference held in Rio one year ago.
I would think my hon. colleagues would recall the excellent communications capabilities provided from that conference and how Canada stood in the forefront around the world. Much of that is indeed to the credit of the work undertaken by Mr. Small.
I think his work is excellent. He is no longer with the department, but we are fully confident that he has performed his requirements very skilfully.

Madam Speaker, I would like to know which facts I have wrong.
There is no denying that Mr. Small is now the campaign manager of the Minister of the Environment. There is no denying that the guidelines require all contracts over $50,000 to be publicly tendered. These were not. The contract was broken into chunks of less than $50,000. There is no denying that Mr. Small was giving image and communications advice and helping to promote the image of the Minister of the Environment who is now a candidate for the leadership of his party.
How am I wrong in suggesting that the taxpayers have been bilked of $200,000 in a Tory leadership race?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
In her speech in Toronto yesterday the Minister of National Defence stated that she wanted to "target social programs". The minister specifically wants to target Canada's elderly by deindexing pensions. As the minister will recall, in 1985 the Prime Minister was told it would be goodbye, Charlie Brown for a similar approach.
Why is the cabinet now targeting senior citizens? Will the minister stand in his place today to repudiate this new policy initiative?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Madam Speaker, I would like to quote the Minister of National Defence. She actually said in Toronto: "We need comprehensive income security reform to make our social programs more effective in helping Canadians to become self-sufficient and to ensure the elderly and the disabled enjoy a decent standard of living as the population ages".
I repeatedly said in the House and outside the House that I believe Canada will soon have to re-examine all its social policies and to adapt them to the realities of 1993. It does not mean that we will necessarily change the policy for older citizens. The minister of defence did not say that she would change them. She said that we would reconsider a range of policies including this one. It is quite possible we will keep them exactly the same.
However, as a government responsible for social policies we believe deeply-and I do as well-that it is time for Canadians to re-examine what it means to change and to re-examine policies. The minister of defence is a responsible person when she says such a thing.

Madam Speaker, the minister will know that no group of Canadians has given as much to this country as senior citizens. No group in this society has worked longer and harder.
I admire the minister for the tough stand he took with regard to the comments made by the Minister of National Defence concerning user fees. I want the minister to stand in his place to repudiate this new policy initiative of the Minister of National Defence which is to target senior citizens as if they were enemies of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Most Canadians are aware this minister has been following with great concern and sensitivity the circumstances of David Spencer from New Brunswick and Christine Lamont from British Columbia who are currently serving very long prison terms in Brazil.
In a published letter to Mr. Spencer's father on April 14, 1992 the minister alluded to a pending completion of a treaty with Brazil for the transfer of offenders. It would permit Mr. Spencer and Ms. Lamont to be returned to Canada in custody to complete their sentences.
Many citizens would appreciate a current summary of the status of that case. Is the proposed treaty nearing completion? What are the prospects for Spencer and Lamont being returned to Canada in the foreseeable future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the treaty the hon. member is referring to concerning the exchange of offenders has passed the justice committee in the Brazilian parliament. It is now moving to a plenary of the lower house. We are given to understand that it will be dealt

with reasonably expeditiously there. It will then move on to the Brazilian Senate and we look forward to early ratification of that treaty.
We are also engaged in assisting with the process regarding the appeal. There are two appeals. One is a constitutional appeal as to the locus of the original trial. We look forward to further news on that front too.
I want to assure hon. members concerning the state of Ms. Lamont's health because there was something alluded to in the other place yesterday about it. We regard this as a private matter and do not comment on it publicly, except I want to assure the hon. member and others we take cognizance of any potential problems that might arise. Could the minister tell us whether he is also lying to the people of Quebec?

Early in May the minister and the deputy premier of Alberta announced the results of a review which identified areas of overlap and duplication between the Governments of Canada and Alberta. This was welcome news to Albertans.
Now that the areas of overlap have been identified what actions are being taken? How soon will Alberta benefit from more efficient government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to report on what I think is a very creative and innovative approach to federal-provincial co-operation, reducing costs of government and reducing overlap.
There are a number of specific initiatives, for example bringing together a single agency for meat inspection and looking at the rationalization of the two geological surveys, one in Alberta and one in Canada. We now have a process moving through to August to develop the actual implementation plans for a lot of these proposals.
In the meantime we are going to look at a number of other areas. We only had a 45-day time frame to do the first review. I think we will identify quite a few more. We have specifically identified $15 million worth of savings as a result of the first review and those $15 million are concrete. I expect we are going to find a lot more, reduce overlap and duplication and improve service to Albertans.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present a number of petitions from my constituents who call upon the government to tighten the Young Offenders Act even more, especially as it applies to violent crimes.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents from Blackstock, Ontario requesting that Parliament reaffirm its commitment toward
seeking the elimination of poverty among Canadian children by the year 2000.

Madam Speaker, at the request of 36 constituents in Rideau County, I wish to table a petition asking the government to hold a referendum on official languages.
Although I do not share the views expressed in this petition, I am glad to do my duty as a member in a democratic country and represent my constituents, although they do not share my views on respecting the language of our two founding peoples and on Canadian unity.

Madam Speaker, I have three different sets of petitions I would like to present.
The first petition concerns the serial killer board game. The petitioners ask Parliament to consider amending the Criminal Code of Canada so that violent and degrading material such as the serial killer board game can be kept from being distributed in Canada.

Madam Speaker, the second petition again comes from numerous members of my constituency. It concerns the question of redress to the Ukrainian Canadians.
The petitioners note that the Prime Minister in October 1992 stated that it was the intention of the government to settle the claim to the mutual satisfaction of the government and the Ukrainian Canadian community.
The petitioners ask that the House of Commons act on this to settle and acknowledge the redress issue to the satisfaction of the Ukrainian Canadians in Canada.

Madam Speaker, the third petition concerns the ongoing tragedy in Bosnia-Hercegovina. The petitioners ask the Government of Canada to put pressure on the United Nations to take more concrete action to stop the genocide and
May 28, 1993

particularly the rape camps and other human rights violations in Bosnia-Hercegovina.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour and duty on behalf of a number of people mostly from Saskatoon to present a petition. It calls on the government to take action relative to the unanimous motion of the House of Commons on September 27, 1991 and settle the acknowledgement and redress issues to the mutual satisfaction of the Ukrainian community and the government.
This issue was raised in a speech by the Prime Minister in October 1992 where he expressed the intention of the government to do this. The petitioners ask the government to proceed in that area.

Madam Speaker, I would like to present some petitions from residents throughout the Okanagan-Shuswap area who are particularly concerned about the possibility of the exploitation of Canadian water resources under both the FTA and the proposed NAFTA.
They are urging the Government of Canada to resolve the uncertainty surrounding the issue through the execution of a separate and binding joint diplomatic agreement ratified by both Canada and the United States stating that nothing in either the Canada-U.S. agreement or the North American trade agreement applies to Canada's water resources in other than bottled form.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition from constituents of the Okanagan-Shuswap, the Enderby area and the north Shuswap from Sorrento and Blind Bay who are particularly concerned about the number of violent incidents that occur on television on a daily basis.
These petitioners ask the government to resolve the issue of violence on television by encouraging communication between the public and the industry, in particular with respect to holding public hearings with recommendations for limitations on the amount of exposure to violent television viewing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to participate in this debate on the opposition day motion.
I am sure it would come as no surprise to my colleagues that I do not agree with the motion. I will have the opportunity to say why. The motion reads:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to protect
Canadian interests regarding the interbasin transfer of water-
It then proceeds to give a number of examples. I will not be able to respond to all the examples. Other speakers this afternoon will carry on with illustrations of how the government has played a very strong role in protecting our water resources.
I would like to talk about the broader issue of what the government's role has been with respect to water issues in Canada.
I believe that the foundation of the government's success, and not its failure as this motion would allege, is in the way that this government has developed, enunciated and implemented a federal water policy within the framework of the Canada Water Act.
Water, both fresh and ocean, is really the foundation of this country's identity, our historical development, our unity and our economic prosperity. It remains so as we move more strongly into an era where environmental sustainability is recognized as a primary force in the formulation of government policies and programs.
Canada possesses approximately 9 per cent of the world's fresh renewable water supply. It flows continuously through some of the world's most significant water basins and through the Great Lakes. Our rivers flow north, east, west and south. We share our rivers and our lakes with our neighbours to the south. For a significant part of our international boundary rivers or lakes are that boundary. Our provinces share our rivers as they often have their head-waters in one province and their estuaries, whether in the ocean or in lakes, in another.
Our rivers and lakes were important transportation corridors for our aboriginal people when they came to this continent many thousands of years ago, as they were for the European settlers who came in the 1500s and the 1600s. We have all read about and seen television
depictions of the voyageurs using these water routes as the mechanism by which they first developed Canada.
Our rivers and our lakes are also recognized as important food sources by all these people. Today we recognize our waters as being more than just transportation corridors and sources of food. We recognize them as being essential ecosystems the health and sustainability of which are essential both to our short-term and long-term futures.
Madam Speaker, you may think I digress by setting this historical context but I think it is apparent from the wording of the motion that it is necessary that the importance of these historical relations be enunciated.
Water management and water policies have been essential in this country from times predating nationhood. Water management and water policies have been of considerable concern to the Parliament of Canada and the Governments of Canada since Confederation.
The role of the federal government is not exclusive in this area of government responsibility. Water as a natural resource is constitutionally the property and prime responsibility of provincial governments to manage and protect.
Nevertheless there are certain heads of constitutional authority on which the federal government can and does exercise powers. For example, we do so under the Navigable Waters Protection Act to ensure that navigable waters, whether rivers or lakes, are protected and preserved for the inherent purposes of water-borne transportation.
We do so under the Fisheries Act to ensure that the fisheries are protected and preserved from over-use, contamination, the construction of dams, dikes, diversions or other structures that might inhibit the migration of fish during the very short course of their lives in some instances.
We also do so under the Canada Water Act, which sets out the basis for federal co-operation with the provinces in all aspects of water management.
We do so under the International River Improvements Act, which is used to ensure that modification to rivers that are international in nature and subject to engineering activities intended to improve and manage their flows are appropriate to the sound principles of water management and environmental sustainability.

May 28, 1993
Supply
Legislation alone is insufficient to ensure good and sound water management policies. Well-considered and developed policies that have the support and approval of the greater proportion of our population and of all levels of government are the key that must guide our governments in the development of operational programs and activities that are intended to ensure the optimal use of our waters within the framework of a sustainable environment.
In 1984 the federal government instituted a major review of its freshwater policy. The Canada Water Act, which has been in place since 1970, like any other enabling legislation requires policies and programs to achieve our federal and national goals. This act, which can still be considered an appropriate legislative basis for action, requires up to date, effective and realistic policies. The review, entitled "An Inquiry on Federal Water Policy", was led by Professor Peter Pearse, an economist at the University of British Columbia who is experienced in renewable resources, has been involved in many inquiries, and is a well-renowned British Columbian.
He held 18 months of hearings, research and consultations with all levels of government in water uses across the country. The inquiry submitted its final report in September 1985. Of the 55 recommendations made by inquiry members, ranging over issues as diverse as northern data networks, organizational change, and project evaluation criteria, I wish to draw the attention of colleagues to two recommendations which relate directly to the hon. member's motion. One concerns interbasin transfers of water within Canada and the other concerns the water export issue.
The inquiry noted that Canada already diverts more water by volume across drainage basin divides than any other country in the world, indeed more than does the United States and the former U.S.S.R. combined.
Such projects are increasingly criticized, despite impressive outputs of electricity, irrigated crops and municipal water supply, because of disruptions to northern, and especially native, communities and to the ecosystems that are their resource base.
The inquiry therefore recommended that interbasin transfers be considered in future only with great caution and only when alternative means of serving their purposes were not feasible.
On the water export issue, the inquiry made two major contributions to the government's further deliberations. The first was to distinguish between small scale exports, such as containerized drinking supplies, and large scale interbasin river diversions, like the North Thompson proposal, with obviously much more serious economic, social and environmental implications.
In forming its response during the following months the government accepted this distinction rather than try to provide one sweeping policy for all situations because they are really quite different in terms of substance and impact.
Second, the inquiry recognized the importance of creating a system for regulating water exports. After two decades in which former governments simply denied interest in water export and hoped that the problem would go away, this government has begun to explore the legislative possibilities along the lines recommended by the inquiry. After extensive review of all of the inquiry's recommendations by provincial governments, public interest groups and individuals the Government of Canada announced a new federal water policy in 1987. This policy statement is both comprehensive in its philosophy and specific in its approach to various water-related issues.
The federal water policy of 1987 represents the first official statement by a federal government in this country to elaborate its approach to water management in general and its policy on water diversion and export in particular. This policy has been welcomed with very few reservations right across Canada.
Let me summarize the government's policy on water transfers within this country and on export to beyond our borders and explain what we are doing to implement this policy.
Hon. members should appreciate that the pace of construction of interbasin water diversions has fallen off dramatically in Canada in the last few years. Our policy advocates caution in projecting the need for major transfers and endorses less disruptive alternatives such as conservation and demand management.
Provincial hydro corporations are benefiting from the economies of this kind of reorientation already, as are the social structure and the ecosystem integrity of many of the northern communities that are protected now
May 28, 1993

from flooding, mercury contamination and biotic change while governments assess the risks of further project construction.
At present the federal government is proceeding to draft guidelines and criteria for assessing interbasin transfer proposals and will review those in co-operation with provincial and territorial governments in the near future.
The federal policy on water export from Canada is direct and explicit. In keeping with the strength of public feeling on this issue, the government will take all possible measures within the limits of its constitutional authority to prohibit the large scale export of Canadian water, as by interbasin diversion, and strengthen federal legislation to the extent necessary to fully implement this policy.
For small scale exports of water, we will work with provincial governments to develop a licensing system which takes into account our respective jurisdictional interests.
Hon. members will recall that the government moved quickly on its commitments related to water exports. In 1988 the Minister of the Environment tabled Bill C-156 to be known as the Canada water preservation act to reassure Canadians that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement will not threaten in any way Canada's sovereignty over its water resources.
Although an election call cut short immediate consideration of this bill, the crisis of public confidence passed and the current environment minister has continued to consult with his provincial colleagues on the possible reintroduction of this or a similar bill which would prohibit large scale and regulate smaller exports of water from Canada.
I wanted to mention one specific aspect of the motion before us because it refers to the North Thompson River-I know an issue of concern to colleagues throughout British Columbia-from which an export of one million acre feet of water to the United States has been proposed by Multinational Water and Power Incorporated.
I can assure my colleague that such an export would clearly be a large scale export and as such is not acceptable to this government. Much of our existing legislation which I mentioned earlier, the Fisheries Act,
Supply
the International River Improvements Act, the Navigable Waters Protection Act and the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act can all be employed if necessary to block this project if we do not have the Canada water preservation act enacted and in place in time to do so.
We believe we have the mechanisms by which we could take action if in fact this project should proceed. I am really not aware at this time that it will because obviously people should be aware that it is not acceptable.
I think it would be appropriate to remind the hon. member who has in his motion despaired of protecting Canadian water resources from manipulation across drainage divides and political boundaries that the situation is far from desperate. The era of megadams and diversions is drawing to a close on both sides of the 49th parallel.
Times are changing. Three months ago the U.S. Geological Survey reported that total withdrawals from surface and groundwater sources in that country has continued a slight decline which began in the mid-1980s. In the dry west, California officials are now projecting no problems in balancing water supplies and demands to the year 2020.
I know that Canadians fear that somehow the United States is going to run out of water and inevitably it will lead to pressure on Canada to share its wealth. I can assure the House the government does not subscribe to the inevitability nor the irresistibility of such pressure. The overwhelming majority of Canadians we know formally oppose it. I think the United States has discovered that it is altogether cheaper in both economic and environmental terms to conserve locally available water supplies and to reallocate them among users by voluntary market transactions. In fact the largest consumptive user in the United States, irrigation, is clearly in decline with conversion of agricultural water rights to urban uses. Recycling has also reduced industrial water demand substantially as well.
We cannot discount the likelihood of major changes in the long term. One of the issues that we are certainly very concerned about in the environment portfolio is climate change, technology or economic development which also might lead to a reconsideration of water demands across this continent. I think it would be

Supply
foolhardy for anyone to predict at this time how either Canada or the United States would choose to respond to such possibilities.
An example is perhaps if temperatures do increase because of the effect of greenhouse gases, and of course we are taking all measures possible to reduce those gases, should Canada divert its northern rivers southward in order to counter higher evaporation rates or should we avoid doing so for fear of increasing the melting rate of the Arctic ice? We simply do not understand those natural processes well enough yet, let alone our capacity to affect or adjust to them to make realistic long-term decisions now.
What government should be doing however is maintaining a watching brief on these events and trends which could affect federal-provincial bilateral relations on the waters that we hold in common. This government maintains a strong focus on major interjurisdictional rivers through joint boards with our provinces and our territories on the Mackenzie, the Yukon, the Saskatche-wan-Nelson, Lake of the Woods, the Ottawa basins. We have joint boards with provincial governments and U.S. representation on our international boundary water basins.
In the next few years for example we will be giving priority to protecting our national interest as we approach the termination of the first hydroelectric power sale under the Columbia River Treaty in 1998. The renegotiation of the Niagara River Diversion Treaty in the year 2000 will also have to be addressed, as will the need to revisit targets for land and water use regulations around the Great Lakes to reduce pollution levels and limit damages from water level fluctuations.
In other words, the long-standing but still evolving relationship between our two countries in dealing with the waters that we hold in common, along and across our boundaries, will continue to have more significance than any prospect for the foreseeable future of exporting Canadian waters to the U.S. markets.
If we continue to exercise our responsibilities to manage water systems in co-operation with other governments, provincial and of course the U.S., water management and policy nevertheless must change with the times. The federal water policy has initiated a
transition period in which we can go beyond reacting to problems and begin anticipating means of avoiding or minimizing them. That is the policy, the basis of the green plan, which builds upon the federal water policy and sets it within a broader, long-term framework of the economy and the environment.
In this perspective, it is important to recognize that the issues are not as simple or as one-dimensional as capturing more water supply for our growing economy. The narrowness of that perspective is what got us into so much trouble over the years. The newer management framework recognizes the tremendous value of our water resources both for our economy and our environment and the urgency of learning to live within the limits of each in the long run and that obviously is what needs to be mutually reinforcing.
I was going to share with colleagues some of the highlights from the green plan which touch upon water and show some of the veiy specific actions, whether it is with the Fraser River basin in my own home province or in Alberta the northern river study. I visited with them recently to see the excellent work that people are doing at the grassroots level and are involved to help protect and preserve some of our most important river basins throughout this country. I applaud so many people who have been involved, not just government people, but local people involved in these various management committees. I think that is what is so important.
I know my time is up, but just let me conclude by saying that there are many aspects of water management and of water policies and programs that the hon. member may have overlooked in presenting his motion. I can assure him that this government has recognized the importance of sound water management, of having clear policies in place, of protecting our legislative basis of action, and of building partnerships with other levels of government and with other stakeholders, some of whom have specific or shared jurisdiction for water management.
The result of all this is a comprehensive and effective approach to water management, an evolving one which takes into consideration broader economic and environmental changes for the purposes of ensuring a healthy
May 28, 1993

and sustainable water resource and aquatic ecosystem throughout this vast and rich land.
I appreciate this opportunity of talking about some of these issues. We do not often get the opportunity in this House. I hope my comments may have helped my colleagues understand the breadth and the depth of our policies with respect to water management.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this issue and I want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, for raising this very important issue. It is important not only to the people of British Columbia but to people throughout Canada.
I am holding a glass of water in my hand. Water as an issue is becoming extremely important, particularly for the residents in my constituency in the Okanagan-Shuswap. The Okanagan-Shuswap is probably one of the only areas in Canada that is semi-arid and people understand the need for fresh water supplies. They understand the concern about the possibility of exploiting Canada's water resources. When they hear that through both the free trade agreement and the NAFTA the government has left itself vulnerable to the exploitation of water through possible export agreements, people justifiably get very concerned.
I have been speaking on this issue for quite some time.
I think that many times in this House I have demonstrated that because of the government's failure to provide specific exclusions for the bulk export of water in the free trade agreement and the North American free trade agreement, it has opened the spill gates to the possibility of major diversions. These may include tanker transport of water off the coast of British Columbia or water diversion schemes as proposed with the diversion of the North Thompson by multinational water resources.
I have been making so much noise on this that the Minister of the Environment, who is currently running for the leadership of this country, was in my riding the other day calling me a liar. I was shocked. I was very concerned about comments. I do not quite know what he has been smoking but I think it has altered his sense of reality.
There was an interesting editorial as a result of the Minister of the Environment's comments that was reported in both the Vernon Daily News and The Morning Star. This editorial opinion states:"It may make for interesting politics but there was not much in the way of substance to environment minister Jean Charest's comments on the water export issue. Charest says that MacWilliam is misleading the public".

It was not quite that way. In the original commentary in both papers he was quoted as saying I was lying about the issue. It states here:"Charest says MacWilliam is misleading the public and that NAFTA only applies to bottled water. This is interesting. What is disturbing about the debate is the government's offhanded manner of dealing with these concerns. If the intent was to exclude bulk water exports from free trade, the government should not be afraid to state that clearly and without reservation. Instead, all we get are vague statements that do nothing to indicate the government's position on this issue".
I found that editorial opinion to be quite refreshing to say the least. I think we have been able to document, and I will do so here again today, the fact that water is included as a commodity of trade in the free trade agreement and also in the North American free trade agreement.
Because water is included as a commodity of trade, the provisions of both those agreements will take precedence over federal water policy or any federal domestic legislation pertaining to water exports.
The government's federal water policy remains nothing but a philosophical document. It has built its defence around this and the fact that the implementing legislation which was just passed yesterday in the House of Commons says that nothing in the North American free trade agreement pertains to bulk water exports.
It is interesting to note that international legal experts have said that it does not matter what our federal water policy says or what our domestic implementing legislation may say. Unless there are specific exclusions for certain items as commodities of trade in this agreement, the conditions or provisions of the NAFTA take primacy over any domestic provincial or federal legislation, policy or otherwise.
It says it does not matter diddly squat what our federal laws or policies say. Unless there is specific exclusion in this agreement then this agreement can override those provisions. It is only this government that has continued to mislead Canadians with its line that water is not included in either the FTA or the NAFTA. It is only this government that refuses to see how its failure to negotiate specific exclusions to water exports in either the FTA or NAFTA has endangered Canada's water resources and has severely compromised our sovereignty on these kinds of resource issues.
I would like to turn to the specific provisions in NAFTA that pertain to water. Under the architecture of both the free trade agreement and the NAFTA-they are very similar-we see that water is included as a commodity of trade. It is specifically mentioned under the tariff schedule as "water including natural or artificial waters and aerated waters-ice and snow".
It is not surprising that this same definition for water shows up in the North American trade agreement. Specifically article 102 of that agreement sets forth the objectives of the agreement to eliminating barriers to trade and facilitating the cross-border movement of goods and services between parties or countries.
Further on, goods of a party-because that is what we are dealing with, trading goods-are identified in article 201 of the North American trade agreement as "products as these are understood in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trades".
Lo and behold, looking at the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and that long list of tariff items, we find article 2201 listing water as "ordinary natural water of all kinds other than sea water".
The only conclusion one can make from that is that water is included as a commodity of trade or as a trade good under both the free trade agreement and the North American trade agreement.
Turning to article 103, which is very similar to article 104 in the FTA, we find that it establishes primacy of the NAFTA over all other agreements or domestic legislation. This is the problem. Without a specific exclusion for water in the agreement and with in fact the express inclusion of water as a commodity of trade and the fact that this agreement takes primacy over our federal water policy, then we have a problem.
Article 301 of the NAFTA says that it requires each party to "accord national treatment to the goods of another party". In other words, the interests of one

Let us look at a specific annex of the North American trade agreement, annex 301.3. The government was not entirely asleep at the switch. At least it had the presence of mind to exclude the export of raw logs. At least it had the presence of mind to exclude the export of unprocessed fish from Quebec and the maritimes. It forgot about the fact that we have a British Columbia fishing industry out on the west coast, but it at least managed to exclude the export of unprocessed fish from central and eastern Canada.
Raw logs and unprocessed fish are excluded. Well, what about the exclusion of bulk water exports? The agreement remains absolutely silent on this. If the government was truly committed to excluding the possibility of future bulk exports of water whether by tanker, pipeline or interbasin transfer, it could have simply slipped in a clause in this section specifically excluding bulk water exports. That would have done the trick. But the government refused to do so in the initial negotiations and it has refused to listen to our requests to do so in the process of possibly amending this particular agreement. Therefore this is where we could have unequivocally excluded bulk water transfers from the North American trade agreement.
Why did the government not do it? One of the senior trade negotiators who was responsible for this section of the agreement said that they did not think it was needed. Well, the international legal experts disagree with that.

Mr. Speaker, the member raises a very pertinent question.
As I said before I fully concede there is nothing in either of these agreements which compels Canada to sell a resource it does not want to sell, but there is nothing in these agreements that expressly prohibits it. Therefore if this government were to have a change of mind tomorrow or the next day and decided that it wanted to change its export policy or its policy on water diversions, it could do so.
Political or economic pressure can be applied from other sources that unless Canada releases a little bit of water there will be a trade war on softwood or a trade war in some other commodity.
Many pressures can be applied economically to try to convince the government to reconsider, which it is already doing, its export policy on water. That is the fear that unless it is specifically prohibited within the agreement itself, the spill gates are open.
We know that California is running desperately short of water, the Colorado River has dried up to a trickle, the aquifers are being pumped down and their water is short. There are many subdivisions in California that have been stopped cold. They cannot proceed with them any further because they cannot get the water provisions to build those subdivisions.
We know the population of southern California is already larger than Canada's and is literally exploding. They are looking for water and they are looking north. All you have to do is read the Equinox article last month on Canada's water supplies.
