speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to contribute a few comments to the debate on the motion presented today by the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley in which he expressed his so-called fears that the Government of Canada was about to sell substantial quantities of water, I suppose we could say in bulk, to the Americans.
In the course of this debate I heard several speeches in this House by members of the New Democratic Party. These members live in another world, another era. They live in an environment that is not ours. They seem to be living in a kind of bubble, completely cut off from the real world and completely oblivious to the changes that are taking place. That must be why they want Canada to be isolated and unable to trade with other countries such as our neighbours to the south.
Yesterday they were against the North American free trade agreement to the very end. They take the position that Canada should not trade with other countries, should not export its products to other countries and should not buy products from other countries. That is the NDP position.
Today's debate is an excuse to say that our drinking water reserves are at risk and that we are about to deplete our natural reservoirs by sending the water they contain to the United States.
I have a simple question for my NDP friends. If at some time in the future, the United States needed a natural water supply to ensure the survival of their people, to give their children the drinking water they need and Canada still had tremendous supplies of water, would we be able to face the international community and deny our neighbours to the south access to our water resources? Would we be able to justify before the highest courts in the world the fact that we refuse to export
water to the United States to help them maintain public health and sanitation and help them continue to provide people in countries to the south with the drinking water supplies they need? Could we defend such a position? That is what members of the New Democratic Party are saying in this House. That is their position. I find that hard to understand. That is why I maintain that our socialist friends opposite are living in a bubble, completely cut off from the real world.
Any substantial interbasin transfers of water for export purposes would clearly contravene the federal government's 1987 water policy. The hon. member suggests that the agreement signed by our government would allow exports of vast quantities of water. That is just not the case.
In its natural state, water is no more marketable than trees in the forest or oil or natural gas in the subsoil. Only when water is collected by taking it out of its natural state and bringing it on the market, for instance by bottling it or shipping it in tanks, does it become a product covered by rules set forth in trade agreements. I think that is perfectly clear.
Interbasin transfers of water are entirely different, because they do not involve the sale of water as a product but the diversion of water in its natural state. Water in its natural state is not covered by international trade agreements, and that includes NAFTA.
The government understands the concerns of Canadians. I noticed that British Columbia, the hon. member's own province, imposed a moratorium on water exports, thus reflecting federal polity. The government's position on water exports is clearly defined in the federal water policy and in the implementation legislation for the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the North American free trade agreement between Canada, the United States and Mexico.
I repeat, nothing in these agreements gives the United States or Mexico access to our water, which means that Canadian governments are, and will continue to be, free to regulate management of our water resources. Tb me that is clear.
The Columbia River and its tributaries are trans border waterways that naturally cross the border between the United States and Canada. Our two countries have for many years shared water and water resources, as officially recognized in the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 at the beginning of this century. In 1909 Canada and

the United States also signed a treaty regulating use of the waters of the Columbia River.
Waters flowing to the United States from the Canadian section of the Columbia River are regulated nor affected by the free trade agreement and will not be affected by the free trade agreement between Canada, the United States and Mexico. The dams on the Columbia River are managed in accordance with the provisions of the Columbia River Treaty by B.C. Hydro, the Bonneville Power Administration and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. We have an agreement that regulates the use of the Columbia River water. The Columbia River Treaty manages a joint resource so as to maximize flood prevention and power production. It does not mention water exports.
As far as water exports are concerned, Canada's position is clearly defined in the federal water policy adopted in 1987. This policy prohibits large-scale exports of water from Canada through the diversion of water from lakes and rivers. So that is clear.
Furthermore, section 7 of the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act clearly provides that nothing in the agreement applies to water, except water packaged as a beverage or in tanks. This legislation has been in effect since January 1, 1989. Similarly, the North American free trade agreement does not include large scale water exports. The North American Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act will include a special clause confirming Canada's sovereignty over its water resources.
Considering recent comments in this House and petitions tabled by members of the New Democratic Party, Canadians may wonder whether, under the North American free trade agreement, Canada will be forced to export water through interbasin transfers.
The answer is: absolutely not. Water transfers on a large scale were not part of NAFTA negotiations. The question was never raised at any level during the negotiations. The Government of Canada-and I said this earlier-has a firm policy on interbasin water transfers and water diversion. The Canadian federal water policy, as I said before, was adopted in 1987 and specifi-

cally prohibits such projects, whether we are talking about interbasin transfers or water diversion.
Why do they keep raising these fears? Why do they keep claiming that the Government of Canada is about to sign or negotiate agreements that will allow large-scale transfers of water to our neighbours to the south? This is absolutely not the case. As I said earlier, the government reserves the right to discuss the possibility or to make arrangements, perhaps on humanitarian grounds, for the transfer of water to our neighbours to the south.
Trade rules only apply to primary resources in their marketable form. For Canada, these rules apply only to water commercially available in bottles, I repeat, or in tanks. NAFTA rules do not apply to our rivers, lakes or other bodies of water.
For how long and how many times will we have to repeat that the statements made in this House by members of the New Democratic Party are unfounded. We must stop frightening Canadians. We must look at things as they are. We must analyse in detail the terms of the free trade agreements with the United States, the terms of the free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico and realize that water transfers and bulk exports of water are not part of them. The agreements do not allow such transfers. Should the need ever arise separate agreements would have to be negotiated. Separate accords would have to be prepared and the terms negotiated so as to continue to ensure that our water reserves are protected and that we always preserve the integrity of our water resources in rivers or lakes for Canadians.
I do not want to take any more of the House's time. I think what I have said is very clear. On our side of the House in any case, we think it is clear because we have read the free trade agreement. We understand the free trade agreements with the United States and Mexico and it is very clear that water is not covered by them, except for bottled water, in the same way that we in Canada can go to a shopping centre or food store and buy water that was bottled in the United States. It is exactly the same thing. The free trade agreements allow transfers or sales of bottled water or water in containers because it has

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to speak on the motion of the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, which reads:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to protect Canadian interests regarding the interbasin transfer of water as exemplified by the Kemano project, the North Thompson River, and both the Columbia River Treaty and the North American free trade agreement.
The events which led to the development and construction of the Kemano project in British Columbia in 1950 are painful memories for the people of the Cheslat-ta Indian band. This shameful period in the history of Canada and British Columbia has not been forgotten. Today the frightening prospect exists whereby history may repeat itself through the prospects of Kemano II and the opportunities which may lay ahead under NAFTA.
In speaking on the issue of interbasin transfers of water and the opportunities for such projects in the future in NAFTA it would be morally and environmentally irresponsible to overlook the overwhelming damage caused by the first Kemano project.
Most important, the project required the removal of the Cheslatta people and the uprooting of fully developed, tightly knit and self-sufficient communities. These people were literally forced off their land with virtually no compensation nor assistance with their relocation or re-establishment.	[DOT]

Their traps, cabins, campsites, trails, trading routes and burial grounds were flooded to make way for the new Nechako reservoir. A whole people, their highly organized culture and traditions which took centuries to evolve were virtually destroyed and lost forever in the flooded waters. That was a very expensive price to pay for the growth of big business and the wealth of a select few.
The social and environmental impacts cannot be overstated. A people and a way of life were destroyed in the process. What else can be said?
The very fact of the matter is that negotiations were undertaken without the consultation and participation of aboriginal peoples. They were forced to deal with the effects of Kemano I after the fact.
It has been alleged that no one ever told the Cheslatta people they had a right to refuse the surrender of their traditional lands. They did not receive third party advice or the opportunity to seek third party advice.
It is difficult to comprehend the licence given to Alcan for this project. British Columbia granted an exclusive water licence to store and direct water flows in the Nechako and Ninika Rivers for the purpose of developing a hydroelectric facility. The licence allowed Alcan to fully divert the Nechako River without the requirement to maintain sufficient water flows to protect fish populations.
Thirty-five per cent of the Nechako River was diverted. The fact that the general public and aboriginal people were not made part of this monumental environmental decision-making process is a travesty.
In 1980 the minister of fisheries at the time, Romeo LeBlanc, issued a minister's order under the Fisheries Act requiring Alcan to increase water flows from Kemano I in order to protect the fishery.
In 1984 fisheries minister Pierre De Bane announced that there would be a full public inquiry into the Kemano II project. However, following the election win of the Conservative government in 1984 the Kemano II project was withdrawn and all plans for a public review were shelved.
Environmental and aboriginal groups were caught completely off guard when in September 1987 the Kemano settlement agreement suddenly endorsed plans for Kemano II. This agreement was negotiated by the then fisheries minister who is now Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. This agreement was mysteriously reached without the involvement of aboriginal communities or public interest groups.
To date Alcan has already invested over $600 million in the development of Kemano II. While it has suspended all work on the project pending the outcome of the B.C. judicial inquiry set to begin this fall, Alcan has stated that should its agreements with the federal government be overruled or affected it will take court action to retrieve full compensation for its investment.
Everyone has mentioned it but it bears repeating. Kemano II is a $1 billion project that when completed will provide a second tunnel between the Nechako reservoir and Kemano. Kemano II will also include a new powerhouse, a new transmission line and a multiport water release mechanism at Kenney dam which will regulate water for migrating sockeye. Water flows to the Nechako will drop sharply. Kemano II reduces the Nechako River to a shadow of its former self.
In a report prepared by David Suzuki for a television special aired in April it was reported that 80 per cent of the Nechako water flow would be diverted, leaving only 14 per cent of the water. Mr. Suzuki also confirmed that this would destroy the salmon run.
Kemano II threatens the freshwater fisheries of the Upper Nechako and four salmon runs directly: the wild Nadina, the Nautley and the Stuart sockeye runs, and the wild, Upper Nechako Chinook.
The reduced flows of Kemano II could lead to a number of Fraser River runs also being hit very hard in years to come. This is according to the department of fisheries Kemano task force and the former international Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission. Most important, Kemano II threatens the food and commercial fishery of dozens of Indian nations.
Interior natives will be forced to travel extended distances to find reasonable salmon stocks. All native people who rely on Fraser and Skeena river watersheds for fishing, hunting, trapping and transportation will be severely impacted from Prince George to Vancouver.

The list of social, environmental and economic impacts this project will have on an estimated 134 bands, an estimated 35,130 people, is overwhelming. These figures only refer to those affected in Canada.
A very credible report by the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Science has indicated that the concern over the prospect of the consideration of water as an economic good within the context of NAFTA is very real. The Rawson Academy report stated:
Without an exclusion, water is certainly part of the agreement. Any good or service covered by a tariff heading annexed to the NAFTA is subject to the rights and obligations set out in the Agreement itself. The large scale movement of water was neither raised nor negotiated during the NAFTA negotiations.
Furthermore, Rawson states that the social and economic costs of large scale water transfer would be extremely high. The costs of compensating people for loss of property and relocation of communities displaced by flooding have been given scant consideration. The burden of these costs would largely fall on Canada's native people who inhabit many of the regions that would be affected by the damming and diversion of northern rivers for water export.
We already have examples of this. A book entitled The Dispossessed by Geoffrey York cited tragic experiences whereby Manitoba Hydro flooded the communities of Chemawawin and Moose Lake. In citing information from Mr. York's book, thousands of hectares of wilderness including about two-thirds of the land on the reserve were submerged in water by the construction of the Grand Rapids hydro dam. The tragedy of Moose Lake is that this was once a thriving prosperous community. A host of serious health and social problems has taken hold of this displaced community due to the loss of its traditional native economy through the flooding.

There has been an increasing pressure in Canada to divert our northern water systems. I want to say a few words with regard to trade. Canada is probably one of the most trade dependent nations in the western industrialized world; in fact next only to Germany. It was West Germany but now Germany is one country.
One of every four jobs in Canada depends upon trade and our exports to other countries. Thirty per cent of all revenues the country receives are trade driven. It is very important the country not only trade but that we have secure access to our major trading partners and that we trade under fair, acceptable rules. The rules should be agreed upon by both sides or under the NAFTA threeway country split. There should be a mechanism recognized by all parties with regard to settling disputes.
First we set down the rules and the rules are agreed upon by the three countries. Second there is the dispute mechanism agreed upon. Of course the main theme of the whole agreement is to reduce trade barriers and tariffs and to do away with anti-dumping, countervailing

The FTA with the United States came into being January 1, 1989. It will take 10 full years to implement it, working slowly over the area of reducing tariffs between the two countries.
If NAFTA, the North American free trade agreement which includes Mexico, the U.S. and Canada, is ratified by the other two countries, it would be implemented January 1, 1994. There will be steps in it that we all agree to on how to alleviate the tariffs and the concerns among our countries.
Let us look at trade. Between Canada and the United States probably $250 billion to $260 billion of trade gets done each year. If we include Mexico and we are dealing with the three countries, we are talking $500 billion of trade per year. That is trade both ways, times three countries, per year, which represents a lot of exports and imports. It represents a lot of jobs in all three countries. subject of trade but under the subject of water diversions and transfers of water from one basin to another. That is what all these various subject areas have in common.
I would like specifically to relate to the question of trade. Before I get into any details I want to recogniize the contributions that a number of my colleagues have made in this debate, not only in this House today but across the country in the last number of months and in some cases the last number of years.
Particularly on the Kemano and the Nechako River and the issues relating to that basin, the member for Skeena, who is not with us at the moment, and the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley have been dealing extensively with this.
One of my colleagues, the member for Kootenay East, is not here today. I know that he would want to be. The reason he is not present and able to participate is that he is en route to Eureka, Montana to participate in a multinational meeting that has regard to some of the very issues of diversion, water conservation and general environmental preservation that are some of the spinoffs of the kind of water diversions that we have had already and that we are afraid of meeting in the future.
I also want to specifically mention my colleague, the member for Okanagan-Shuswap, who has contributed already to this particular debate. Along with his colleague for Kamloops he has been engaged to a very great degree in the debate over the proposed diversion of the North Thompson River.
To this point in the debate there have been numerous diversions and picky arguments about the fallaciousness or otherwise, of various statements about the exact words on page x of the free trade agreement, page y of the North American free trade agreement or page z of GATT-I made sure I got the Canadian pronunciation- as to whether water is specified or is not specified and in what way.
I would like to try to avoid some of those picky arguments, as important as some of them are. The government says it is very proud that it has declared a policy. I am glad it has and I congratulate the government for it. It is saying it has no intention as a matter of
policy of approving the large scale export of Canadian water. Fine.
One would have to be pretty dumb not to realize, if one had ever travelled to the American southwest or ever tasted fresh water from the Pacific northwest of Canada, that sooner or later in the not too distant future there are going to be pressures brought to play that are going to make any announced policy of a government appear as nothing more than a puff in the wind no matter what government is elected.
Quite frankly I do not care, coming from the West Kootenays, whether it is a Tory government, a Liberal government federally or provincially, a Socred government, an NDP government, a Reform government or whatever. The fact is that the tremendous resources of water we have available, especially in the southeast corner of British Columbia, comprise almost 2 per cent of the world's supply of fresh water.
If one goes to the American southwest, no matter what hotel one walks into, the sign in any bathroom say "shut the tap off, our water is in danger". Any highway, any little rural road one walks down the signs read: "preserve our water, there is a shortage". They are almost in a state of panic. Anybody who thinks an announced government policy, regardless of the stripe of that government, is going to protect this resource in the face of that kind of pressure is smoking the kind of stuff that a couple of our leadership candidates have made famous recently, not to mention one of my colleagues in the far comer of my own caucus.
They are just floating on cloud nine. Southern California has a population bigger than Canada's. Compare that to British Columbia and particularly southeast British Columbia. My own riding has the smallest population of any electoral district in the province of B.C.
In the last redistribution we only saved that riding and the riding of Kootenay East because both Mr. Brisco, my predecessor from the Conservative Party, and I jointly fought against the redistribution report. More than anything else, we were afraid that if the original report had been adopted we would have had only one member speaking for all the water in the whole southeastern comer of the province.
We needed as many allies as we could get. We successfully fought that redistribution so we could maximize the number of representatives we would have who
May 28, 1993

could protect that resource which we knew would be under attack.
There is a tremendous lack of water in the U.S. southwest. The signs are everywhere in hotel rooms and on the roads.
In that comer of British Columbia we have the biggest storehouse of fresh water in the world with the smallest population. It is simply a matter of leverage. Whether the pressure comes 5 years, 10 years, 20 years or 50 years down the road, the biggest market for Canada is the United States.
The Prime Minister and the minister of trade are very fond of saying we are a trading nation and they are right. Thirty per cent of our economy is based on trade as opposed to maybe 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the United States. Regardless of the agreements we are subject to trade pressure from our American neighbours who are usually our good American neighbours, but they have needs to fulfil also.
We are subject to their needs on a wide variety of fronts. Some day they will be desperate and they are getting close to being desperate in the American southwest. The target may be steel, lumber or electric power generation. Regardless of what price they will pay, where it is going to go or what the commodity is the threat will be that we give them what they need, for a price, or they will cut us off.
In the face of the kind of pressures we are going to get over the next 15, 50 or 75 years, no announced government policy is going to matter a damn. That is why it is such a waste of time to hear the kind of defence that we have a policy.
Right on.

Even if it were a written policy it would not matter very much. Whether or not we are going to export and have large scale diversions of water it will not really matter if it is in or out of an international agreement or not. Even if we wrote it into our Constitution, sooner or later a diversion will happen. The pressures will be so great that no government of whatever stripe will be able to resist them.
We must take whatever steps are humanly possible now to exclude it from the North American free trade agreement. Even though we have passed it through the
Supply
House of Commons we are not necessarily finished with it yet. To exclude it as a good to be considered, we will need all the leverage we can get to demand as high a price as possible.
People will say, and I say rhetorically, there is no price big enough. When we get the kind of pressures that we know we are going to be faced with, because of that expanding U.S. population and our relatively small population, we had better make sure it is going to be virtually impossible for them to do. The federal government, the provincial governments and perhaps other international partners must have the required agreements if we are going to exact the maximum possible price.
The only kind of price that should be considered is probably major geographical concessions in return for that water. Otherwise we are not going to have a country left. Later on we would have to get part of the property, whether it is in the state of Washington or the state of Oregon, in exchange for that kind of water to make sure we are still in a position to benefit from the water we have.
That is how serious it is going to be down the road. It is the kind of issue that nations go to war over. If you want to talk to people who feel it is that kind of issue, come out to the west where we have had to face problems even from something as relatively innocuous as the Columbia River Treaty. It was supposed to have all kinds of safeguards in it and supposedly was limited to simply storage for the purpose of the generation of electric power.
We know what the stakes are and anybody who travels in the American southwest knows what the stakes are. I really do not have much patience with the kind of picky little defences I hear; that it is a government policy or it is not in clause x of this or clause y of that or somewhere else.
As I said, these are the kinds of issues that nations live, die and go to war for. The United States can bring pressures upon Canada, even being the best of friends, if we do not yield for a price somewhere down the road.
I find it patently ridiculous to have anybody on that side lecture us about being realistic in the face of what any school kid ought to know if he or she can count. That is what I meant about the hon. member's argument being

May 28, 1993
Supply
so narrow it was like a river running on its edge. That puts it exactly into perspective.
In the moments available to me I would like to comment on some of the issues raised by my good colleague, the member for Kootenay East or what used to be Kootenay East-Revelstoke prior to the last redistribution.
Last year and again this year in Kootenay East an issue arose that revealed exactly how Canada loses some of its sovereignty when it sells control of its fresh water resources to the U.S. or any foreign nation for that matter.
The Koocanusa reservoir was created when the Libby dam in Montana was built to harness the flow of the south flowing Kootenay River, a branch of the Columbia River in southeastern B.C., as part of the massive Columbia River treaty system.
I am quite familiar with that waterway. It runs right by my home. Until recently the reservoir has been managed relatively well ensuring power benefits and a solid fish and tourism base on both sides of the border.
Last year however the U.S. took water from the reservoir earlier than normal. The B.C. government had to scramble within the narrow range of the treaty to adjust other reservoirs in order to protect the Koocanusa for the . crucial summer season.
Some of those other reservoirs that were partially sacrificed were within my own constituency. We are already facing pressures on those reservoirs again this year even though the shortage on a short-term basis is not quite as drastic in the U.S. southwest as it was last year.
This year water levels are even lower and the Americans are determined to take what is theirs legally not just for power and flood control but also for fish and environmental enhancement. The B.C. government remains restricted under the treaty and the result is that the Koocanusa reservoir is now a dust bowl. The local tourism based economy will be destroyed this summer.
This is a serious issue and shows on a very micro scale the tremendous damage that can result if we allow any large scale diversions of water whether they are supposedly for electrical generation or whatever purpose.
Certainly it was meant for fresh water consumption in the American southwest.
My colleague, the member for Kootenay East, is en route right now to Eureka, Montana to participate in a number of these meetings that have been set up in part to widen the scope of the purposes of that treaty. What is happening?
Water diversion may have originally been for electrical generation but it is now for much more and understandably so. It is legitimately so from the point of view of our American neighbours across the way who are concerned about their quality of life and that of their children in the future.
We are not their enemies. We have to live together. Sooner or later we are going to have to make accommodations for humanitarian purposes and because the negotiating pressures will be so great. We will have to find a price and conditions acceptable to both our good neighbour and Canada, living just a few miles apart.
I appeal to the government once more. Regardless of its exact, fine, narrow range arguments about whether something is in this treaty, this clause or not, realize that Canada is here we hope for a long time. Canadians are here we hope for a long time.
We need every bit of ironclad protection as is humanly possible to ensure that whatever government, Liberal, Tory, NDP or Reform 50 years down the road will be forced to get virtually unanimous agreement in order to exact the highest possible price and the strongest possible conditions on the future exports that we know will happen whether we think it is a good idea or not.
That is a reality and I ask the government to face up to it. It has tried to face up to some others but this is perhaps the biggest reality and the toughest crunch that Canadians are ever going to have to face. We need all the weapons we can get. I appeal to them to look ahead and begin now to address those needs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the member's comments and in particular the comments he made about the Columbia River Treaty.
My interest in this particular issue comes from the eastern end of my constituency which just approaches
May 28, 1993

the border of Alberta where Kinbasket Lake, known to many perhaps as the Mica dam reservoir, is the top end of the Columbia River system.
Recently on part of the tour of the interior of British Columbia conducted by members of the interior caucus of New Democrat MPs, we visited the Revelstoke dam which is an important dam in the entire system. B.C. Hydro officials suggested to us that it was one of the most efficient dams in their entire system.
As well there are the U.S. authorities drawing down a great deal of water south of the border, as they are entitled to do under the Columbia River Treaty, creating the problems identified by my colleague and the need of B.C. Hydro to maintain a high level of water behind the Revelstoke dam. These spell great concern for Kinbasket Lake.
On a visit to the lake just a week or two ago, we had to drive some 30 kilometres down a dry lake bed before coming to the point where there was water. The reservoir is just rising now. Hydro officials have advised us that if we do not have a heavy rainfall this fall and a heavy snow pack Kinbasket Lake is going to probably be even lower next summer. We could have some very severe problems because of that.
The hon. member has already mentioned how our other colleague from the Kootenays is travelling to have some consultations with the U.S. legislators and others. As it relates to the Columbia River Treaty, I ask if there is more that can be done in terms of advising and informing the public of this?
The regional district in my area is hosting a public meeting in Valemount. I understand there are some meetings to be planned in the Kootenays. Obviously the public has to be involved. What more can we do to ensure that the public has the full range of information needed on this most important issue?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley for the question. Indeed there are a number of meetings, seminars and conferences being planned throughout West Kootenay and East Kootenay in the coming weeks and months. I am also glad to hear that there are meetings going on in his area.
These meetings are being set up not only on the volition of a number of New Democrats who have been concerned politically for some time, but also by the provincial power agencies and others concerned with the
Supply
administration of the treaty. This is being done to ensure that whatever decisions we do make and whatever lobbies we do mount are done with the greatest amount of knowledge as to exactly what those agreements are and exactly what limitations we are forced to work within.
I would like to pay tribute to some of my predecessors of two parties in my own area, particularly the squire of the Kootenays, Mr. Bert Herridge, who was the member from 1945 to 1968. During the negotiations of the Columbia River Treaty Mr. Herridge did so much to fight what he thought were the bad provisions of that treaty and on balance the treaty as a whole.
Another tribute goes to a predecessor from 1968 to 1974, the member for Kootenay West, Mr. Randolph Harding, who was also a provincial member. I think he destroyed three or four of his own cars travelling around to the communities that were to be flooded. He added his voice to this and did so much, together with a later member, Mr. Brisco, my alter ego with whom I bounced ideas back and forth on numerous occasions.
All of us, in our own time and in our own way, have done what we could to keep our people informed and to try to get the reality as opposed to the myth of the agreement established in people's minds so that we are bargaining with facts and not simply with emotions. It has probably been deduced not just from my tone but from that of my colleagues and some members on the other side that the emotions run as deep and as strong as do the waters and the generating capacity of the area from which I come.

Mr. Speaker, I have some comments leading into a question.
Canada has about 25 per cent of the supply of the world's fresh water but what people do not understand is that most of that is locked up in the form of glaciers in the polar ice cap. We really have only about 9 per cent for a 7 per cent land mass, so we have about our fair share.
The problem is that the majority of that water, about two-thirds of it, flows north. When the United States looks at Canada as this great resource basket for fresh water supplies it is really quite misleading. There is no such thing. Any ecologist will say that there is no such thing as surplus water.

Supply
Any water moving through an ecosystem, a river, is really a living thing. Any water moving through an ecosystem is providing a specific purpose. Once a significant quantity of that water is removed from the ecosystem, irreparable changes to the ecosystem are initiated, many of them very deleterious. That is what really concerns us.
For my colleague from Kootenay West and our other members of the interior team, throughout the interior section of British Columbia, from the northern and central interior through the southern interior into the Kootenays, water is a major issue of concern to our constituents. They understand water issues. They have seen the effect of the Columbia River Treaty. They have seen the effect of the Nechako diversion projects. All of us understand the importance of water as a resource and the vulnerability of this precious resource under the provisions of both the FTA and NAFTA.
This brings me to a short quote and then my question. I received a report, "NAFTA and Water Exports" from the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Sciences. It quotes the Centre for International Environmental Law in Washington, D.C. It states: "Despite the controversy that arose over the FTA, Canadian negotiators did not seek a specific exemption in NAFTA for water and as a result the actual text of NAFTA supports the claim that large scale transfers of Canadian water to the United States and Mexico cannot be prevented".
I would like to get the member's views on that particular quote.

Mr. Speaker, it will not come as any great surprise to you or to members on the other side that I agree with the warning my colleague has just described.
Many people in the Kootenays have been engaged in this discussion and debate and numerous readings of both the text or partial text of the North American free trade agreement and prior to that, the long debate on the free trade agreement. The issue that concerned those people and me the most was whether or not our waters would be protected, how well and for how long.
I would agree that the problem is not that the agreement states that we will export water or that it is
going to be a commodity for the purposes of trade, but that the government for whatever reason has failed to give our waters the same degree of protection as has been given to raw logs, as important as the issue of raw logs exports is. It has failed to accord the same protection as it has done to processed fish, as important as the fishing industry is.
Even though we do not sell water on a large scale now, it is an important commercial commodity as well as being much more than a commercial commodity.
We would appeal once more that when the time comes for an early renegotiation of the terms of NAFTA, because we suspect that is what we are going to see as a result of what happens in the U.S. Congress and elsewhere, that we insert that protection. That would give future governments as much bargaining leverage and power as they can get to exact the highest possible price and the strongest possible conditions when we are faced with an offer we simply cannot refuse.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to participate in this debate. As many of the speakers have already pointed out, water is one of those resources which acts as a lifeline or the life-blood for this nation as well as many other nations.
It probably strikes very much into the core and psyche of this country because so much of our industry, so much of our livelihood and so much of our well-being has been drawn from our very rich and abundant raw resources. It is something that Canadians believe is part of their heritage and part of their culture. It is part of the specific distinctiveness we share in this part of the continent.
I hope that the mover of the resolution does not mind if I extend the debate beyond the concern that he expressed about transfers of water within the British Columbia region, because the same problem is evidenced right across Canada.
In my own part of the country, the prairies, we also have the Assiniboine diversion, the Garrison diversion, the Rafferty-Alameda dam situation and the Oldman dam, all of which are irrigation projects linked up to water basins shared in the United States.
May 28, 1993

The same thing applied in the Great Lakes of Canada. There have been numerous disputes and concerns raised over the years about the sharing of water. As we know, there already are diversion projects such as Lake Michigan into the Chicago system which we have not been able to exercise control over.
This is a national issue. It is one that certainly enough evidence has been put forward in the House to demonstrate that there is legitimate concern about the future pressure we will face because of the increasing demand and shortage of water in the United States.
Because of the trade agreement signed, there is a very large question mark, a very serious doubt as to whether Canada would be in a position to protect and decide for itself on the use of its water without being required to live up to legal obligations under the trade agreements. I would like to just reiterate why this is a concern and not something that is being provoked because of fearmong-ering, as the member from Calgary said, but because of the actual wording of the agreements.
It begins in the free trade agreement and is repeated in the North American free trade agreement. The national treatment clause means that each party shall, to the extent provided in the agreement, accord national treatment with respect to trades in goods and services. It is very clear. We have to treat goods and services trade in the United States exactly as our own. We cannot provide discriminatory pricing, discriminatory quotas or discriminatory quantitative agreements.
Article 409 defines what is a good. It states that article 409 applies to exports of goods. The goods of a party means domestic products as these are understood in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Article 2201 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade includes all natural water, even water as ice and snow, regardless of how it is packaged to transport it.
To follow the logic through, we must afford national treatment to all goods and services. Goods are defined as having the definition given under the GATT. Article 2201 of the GATT defines natural water, including ice and snow, as a good.
Furthermore, in article 408 of the free trade agreement, again repeated in the NAFTA agreement, we have specifically given away the right of Canada to use an export tax which would be the last line of defence.
Supply
We have taken away perhaps one of the most significant trade tools of any country which is to say that before any good is exported to another country we have the right to impose a tax which could be prohibitive to the point where the export would not take place.
We gave up that right with trade with the United States. We retained it for all other countries, but in section 408 we surrendered the right to impose an export tax. As we saw a few years ago with the issue on the west coast salmon because of the surrender of that export tax we could not protect the processing of our own natural resource in our own country.
I went through that legal dissertation for one important reason. The government could clarify the matter instantaneously. All it would have to do is have included in the agreement the exclusion of water, as it did with logs and fish.
It seems to me that after having gone, through the debate in 1988 on the free trade agreement when it came time to negotiate the North American free trade agreement it would have been the most natural thing for a Canadian government that is clearly interested in protecting water resources in Canada to put that on the table with the Americans and Mexicans. It should have said that we have a serious question mark in our country and a lot of very respected analysts and commentators have raised questions about it so let us include water as an exclusionary item.
It did not do it. It did not include it, even though it had a second chance. This is one of the reasons that, as we heard our own leader say in the House a day or so ago, we need a renegotiation to ensure that we do not eliminate these kinds of important items.
If I can add a further concern to the matter. A Winnipeg lawyer and environmentalist by the name of Brian Pannell serves on one of the advisoiy committees to the Minister for International Trade. He is not somebody who is a way-out opponent of the government. He has been a member of the advisory committee of the minister of trade. Just recently, a short month ago, he raised serious questions in a letter to the minister and to the chief negotiator for NAFTA, John Weekes, about the problem of water.

May 28, 1993
Supply
He points out that Canada can restrict water exports only to the extent that it restricts its own domestic use. Under these agreements Canada is bound to the proportional sharing of water. That means that even in times of scarcity Canada must continue to provide the same amount of water in total as its average exports over the previous 36 months.
A member of the trade minister's own advisory committee has raised this concern. It is a legitimate concern because, as the members from British Columbia have pointed out, we now see the problem in the Columbia River flow as the United States is increasing its own use of that water contrary to the spirit of the Columbia River agreement.
Now it will become locked into law as a requirement even in the kind of drought British Columbia experienced last year, in which its own municipalities had to go on short, restricted supply. That is a condition that could happen again, who knows. The environmental experts are talking about environmental warming and all the rest of it. Who knows what the climate will bring.
If we reach a stage in British Columbia, the prairie basin and other areas where we want to use more of our own water for the purposes of our own citizens we would be prevented from making that decision because of these agreements.
That is not something that has been concocted or fantasized. That is in the legal wording of the agreements.
A member of the minister's own advisory committee is raising the same concern and saying: "Please do the right thing and renegotiate the agreement to exclude that issue, get it off the table so that it will not be a concern and it will not be an area of conflict or disturbance between ourselves and the United States".
It is legitimate for us to ask members of the government why they did not do it. The minister of trade participated in the debates in 1988. He knew what the concerns were. He was part of that whole negotiation. Yet when the time came for him to exercise his responsibility in the renegotiation to NAFTA it was not part of the Canadian agenda.
Now the United States is raising serious questions about side agreements on the environment. The President of the United States says: "I want to see what we can do to ensure better protection of our environmental standards". What a proper opportunity for Canada to put the water issue back on the table in the renegotiation of the side agreements.
Will they do it? That is the question.

That is the question because as I listened to the debate over the last week, in report stage and in third reading, there was no mention whatsoever by the minister of trade that he had any intention of including an exclusion of water as part of discussions with the United States on these so-called side agreements.
The door is still open. It is still there. There is an opportunity. I do not understand for the life of me when a government is in such a precarious position, at the end of its mandate and subject to a lot of criticism about its handling of the NAFTA dispute because of the way it pushed it through Parliament, that it would not do the right thing.
I do not understand why the government does not do it, when it knows that it is a reasonably easy, proper, and good thing to do. Unless there is another agenda. Unless there is something it is not prepared to say. The defence I heard from the member from Calgary and others in this debate is that Canada established a water policy in 1987. We had a debate in the House then. What the hon. member did not mention to members of this House and to Canadians is that the trade agreements supersede that policy.
If the United States sometime in the future, next year or the year after, decides it wants to exercise its legal right as contained in the agreements to require Canada to export up to the proportion then it would supersede any policy that is now on the books.
I am going to make the case this afternoon in the time remaining to me that we try to come to an agreement on this. I do not think that it has to be a bare knuckle, hard ball conflict with the United States. We have used the International Joint Commission for decades now to resolve our problems. We have some good architecture between ourselves and the United States to resolve border problems.
May 28, 1993

There is an area in which the whole discussion of water could receive a full hearing. It could be subject to public discussion and public examination. It could bring the United States and Canadians together. We could work out a proper sharing of our border problems. By the way, the problems are not just one way. The dumping of sewage into the Juan de Fuca Strait is a problem the Americans face. As good neighbours we should also be prepared to put that on the table and negotiate that with them.
It is fair that we have quid quo pro and good bargaining arrangements. The Americans have some legitimate disputes about the way we have handled our problems in the Great Lakes. I do not think we have been that good in dealing with the zebra mussel problems. Another funny little fish is running around that is now chewing up game fish. We have not been doing our part of the bargain.
The pollution of the Columbia River.

The pollution of the Columbia River, absolutely. There are mutual interests in coming to a serious discussion, and I would suggest through the International Joint Commission.
In my area we share the Red River basin with the midwestern states. I have suggested for two years that we bring the provinces, the municipalities, the federal government and the United States government together to work out a proper use of that water basin. We all share it and we all need it, yet it is highly polluted by both sides of the border and by two or three provinces and municipalities in those provinces. We are ruining one of the very exquisite resources of the prairies simply by neglect and negligence.
There is room. I think the mover of the resolution would agree that this could be a subject of serious discussion, particularly when there is a new administration in the United States with a vice-president who has written one of the classic books on the environment. It understands this joint concern. We are not dealing with the kind of mentality we saw in the previous administration in which environment was a dirty word.
President Reagan said that the whole problem of trees is that they put CO2 in the air. The level of understanding about the environment has increased substantially
Supply
since that statement was made. There is now an environmentally conscious U.S. administration.
It is one that I thought took a very courageous stand a month or so ago when the new secretary of the interior attempted to impose some serious conservation requirements on federal water uses in the western states. He has been beaten back in the Senate but nevertheless it is making that case. It demonstrates to us that there is room for a serious, open and honest exchange between ourselves and the United States about this very rare continental water resource.
It can only happen and should only happen when Canada is prepared to recover its proper legal rights to protect its water resources. That is a precondition for any serious negotiation. Right now we would be in the classic position of going to a bargaining table with no chips to bring to it because we have allowed them to be bargained away.
I think the debate this afternoon is a very important one if for no other reason than that there is still time for this House to go on record. I fully endorse the proposals dealing with the North Thompson River, the Columbia River and the other water basins in British Columbia because they are feeling the problem most acutely, but it is a problem shared by other parts and regions of Canada. Therefore this House could go on record as suggesting to the government that while the Americans are still open for negotiation on the environmental accords let us get down to Washington as quickly as possible and put it on the table.
It is not a matter of partisan differences among ourselves, the Conservatives and whoever. This is a matter that I think all Canadians can agree to. It is something from which there is no political gain one way or the other. It is just good common sense.
I would think the Canadian people would like to see this Parliament express itself with good common sense, especially on an issue as vital to our livelihood and our future as the protection of our water.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest and learned, as is usual from my colleague from Winnipeg, about the extensive damage that could be done to the water system

Supply
and the ecosystems of Canada. I had also listened to my colleague from Okanagan-Shuswap.
My hon. colleague is a very good organizer and planner and has demonstrated his capacity to lead as a minister in past governments. I would like to ask him: If he were the minister what activities would he undertake or would he see that the cabinet undertook to ensure the protection of our water resource, which is a precious resource and is not an unending renewable resource? What would he recommend as the first steps to be undertaken?

Mr. Speaker, I think the very first item would be that the federal government could make it very explicit that the present moratorium on water exports that the British Columbia government has introduced is the policy of Canada. The federal government should very clearly take an immediate position on that question.
There are a number of quite mischievous proposals in front of it. I have in my hand one from Multinational Water and Power Inc. of Vancouver, B.C., which has a number of plans for the diversion of run-off waters from British Columbia to the west coast of the United States.
I think the federal government should make its position very clear. British Columbia's officials are not sure what the federal position is. The Minister of the Environment, if he is available and interested considering his other preoccupations, should do something about this right away. This could be done tomorrow. It would end the uncertainty if it put these kinds of proposals, such as the the Grand Canal and the Multinational Water project, to rest by saying: Sorry, that is not in the cards.
Second, as I said in my address, and I think this could happen without any hesitation, we should be making a direct proposal to the United States administration that in looking at the new environmental accords as part of NAFTA that we include the exclusion of water as part of that accord. Make that very explicit and very clear. That should be on the table right now. That is not taking into account my other reservations about NAFTA. I am talking about this government here right now. The member asked me if we were there if that is what we would do.
Third, I would think that it would be very important that we engage the Americans in a broad-based discussion of our water resources continental in using the
International Joint Commission. Give it that responsibility to open up a broad-based examination of the water resources.
Fourth-and the list does not get too long-I would sit down with the province of British Columbia in particular and work out a proper negotiating strategy dealing with the Columbia Water Route Royal Treaty, which is coming up for renegotiation in three or four years.

I want to take a minute or two to reflect on some of the thoughts that the previous speaker just gave. He suggested that if we were exporting water that we would have to continue to share that water with the United States. At the present time we are diverting no water for export. There is no reason to suggest that we will ever have to or ever be forced to.

Canadians have no obligation to feed the hungry of the world unless they want to. We choose to do so through normal commercial sales and through some of our foreign aid assistance. However we have no hard obligation to do that.
There are thirsty people in the world today who are short of water for whatever reason. At the present time and certainly not in the foreseeable future we will not choose to export water in any major diversion way. We have no obligation to do so.
If some future government long after all of us here today have left these Chambers choose to make those changes there is nothing we can do to stop them. If we put it into the form of legislation they can change the legislation in a matter of days or weeks. If it is put into a trade agreement and at some future date the United States or Mexico needs that, it can be changed very quickly if the Canadian government of that day and the American or Mexican government of that day want to change it.
The arguments that have gone on here, while they may make good politics and might sound like common sense today, certainly can be changed very quickly by future politicians or policy makers. Quite frankly, since there is no water being traded, all the discussion that we just heard about NAFTA, FTA and GATT simply does not apply to today's situation.
The previous speaker mentioned the problems associated with the Columbia River. He dragged those problems into the sharing of water as it might occur under wording of the free trade agreement. There again it simply does not apply. The Columbia River is a shared basin between Canada and the United States. The Columbia River Treaty does not affect the amount of water that flows into that basin. Whatever is there flows through it.
That brings me to the topic that I wanted to cover today. That is the issue of the Columbia River Treaty which is mentioned in the motion as exemplifying the failure of the Government of Canada to protect Canadian interests regarding interbasin transfers of water.
I will address the issue directly in my comments. However, in doing so I will provide a brief description of the purpose and jurisdiction of the treaty to prevent any misunderstanding of it. Members will clearly see that the benefits under the Columbia River Treaty do not include

May 28, 1993
Supply
interbasin transfers of water. I repeat, do not include interbasin transfers of water.
The Columbia River Treaty benefits are based on the use of water in the existing river system for water flowing downstream as it always has. The U.S. gets no more water or no less water than it would have without the treaty except for the fact that dams constructed under the treaty keep the water in Canada longer than would otherwise be the case and make it available for recreational purposes.
The Columbia River is the fourth largest river in North America in terms of length and quantity of flow. The flow can be extremely variable with summer flows exceeding winter flows by up to 99 times. The large flow and variability of the flow provide unique opportunity to build storage reservoirs to even out the flow to provide flood control and produce electricity.
The Columbia River Treaty is an agreement between Canada and the United States that provides for the development of the Columbia River basin for flood control and power generation. It provides for the co-operative management of the river system to maximize the benefits shared by both Canada and the United States. These benefits are in excess of those that either country could achieve through any sort of unilateral development.
In this case the background is both interesting and pertinent to the motion. I will briefly explain the Columbia River basin and the treaty itself.
The Columbia River basin covers an area of 259,000 square miles. Fifteen per cent of the basin is located in southeastern British Columbia. The remaining 85 per cent extends into the northwestern United States and covers western Montana, most of Idaho, Washington, Oregon and small areas of Wyoming, Utah and Nevada. The basin includes the municipalities of Trail, Kimberley, Cranbrook in British Columbia, as well as Portland, Oregon and Spokane, Washington and Boise in Idaho.
From its source in the Columbia Lake, 80 miles north of the U.S. border, the river flows northwest to a point about 225 miles from the border then almost due south past Revelstoke and Trail into the United States. Then it
flows first south through Washington and then west to the Pacific Ocean at Astoria, Oregon.
Of its total fall in elevation of 2,650 feet from the Columbia Lake to the sea, 1,360 feet occur it Canada and 1,290 in the United States. This combination of head, or drop in elevation, and the large flow make the Columbia River one of the greatest rivers for hydroelectric power in North America. These flows however are highly variable with 75 per cent of the average flow occurring in the summer months of May through August.
Another major river in the basin is the second largest tributary of the Columbia and that is the Kootenay River. The Kootenay flows south from the Alberta-Brit-ish Columbia border, past the head of the Columbia River at Canal Flats, British Columbia where the Kootenay is approximately one mile from the Columbia River and at roughly the same elevation. It then flows into Montana and Idaho, northward again through British Columbia to Kootenay Lake from which it then drains into the Columbia River. Three-quarters of the drainage area of the Kootenay and two-thirds of its 464-mile length are in British Columbia.
Two other American rivers drain into the Columbia. The average annual flow of the Columbia River at its mouth is 180 million acre feet or about 270,000 cubic feet per second. Approximately 35 per cent of the flow emanates from the Kootenay River and the Canadian portion of the Columbia River. The remaining 65 per cent comes from the American portion of the river basin.
The Columbia River Treaty was originally signed in 1961 but was not ratified until 1964. Under the treaty Canada agreed to construct three storage dams on the Columbia River; to operate the treaty storages so as to maximize flood control and power benefits realized downstream at U.S. hydroelectric plants; and to allow flooding along 42 miles of the Kootenay River for the reservoir required for the Libby dam which the United States planned to build in Montana.
At that time Canada received $64.4 million for 60 years of flood control benefits and one-half of the additional power generated in the United States from the operation of the treaty dams in Canada for a period of at least 60 years.
May 28, 1993

In 1963 the Governments of Canada and British Columbia signed an agreement that gave British Columbia responsibility for building and operating the Canadian treaty dams in return for flood control payments and permanent rights to Canada's share of the power benefits.
Operating entities have been designated by each government to administer the day to day operation of the treaty dams. B.C. Hydro is the Canadian operating entity.
In 1964 British Columbia sold the first 30 years of power benefits to a group of U.S. utilities for $254.4 million U.S. The payments received as a result of this treaty were significant sums in the mid-1960s.
Canada's share of the power benefits, initially sold to the United States, are to be returned to Canada starting in 1998. The 30-year sales agreement expires in phases over a five-year period beginning March 31, 1998 because the power benefits began to accrue to Canada as the treaty dams were completed in 1968, 1969 and 1973. Therefore the first block of treaty benefits will return to British Columbia beginning April 1, 1998 and continue for 30 years.
The principles for calculating the benefits are set out in the treaty documents and British Columbia will ensure that it receives full power benefits to which Canada is entitled.
The operation of the treaty is overseen by a permanent engineering board. This joint Canada-U.S. board reports annually to the Canadian and U.S. governments. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tables the report in the House of Commons.
The climate of the Columbia River basin ranges from moist, mild maritime conditions near the mouth of the river to near desert climate in some of the inland valleys. The Cascade Mountain range separates the coast from the interior of the basin and has a strong influence on the climate in both areas.
There are two important run-off patterns in the basin, the snow melt run-off in the interior east of the Cascade Mountain range and the rainfall run-off of the coastal drainage west of the Cascades. In both areas most of the precipitation occurs during the winter months.
Supply
East of the Cascades most of the precipitation falls as snow in the mountains. Snow accumulates and water is held in natural storage until temperatures rise causing spring run-offs. Spring flows begin to rise in mid-April, reaching a peak flow during May or early June.
Fluctuations in stream flow are caused by the variations in sunlight and air temperature. Occasionally rainfall adds to the run-off. Rain and snow melt over the low lying portions of the basin in the winter can raise stream flows and cause flooding along the lower Columbia and in some of the tributaries.
Originally the two dominant functions of the reservoir system in the Columbia River basin were power generation and flood control. Others added in recent years include the need to maintain high flows in certain periods to aid the downstream migration of juvenile salmon and steelhead and the need to maintain lake levels for resident fish and summer recreation.
The demand for water from the reservoirs for power generation occurs throughout the year. It reaches a peak in the winter when homes and businesses need heating. Demand in the summer is the lowest. Thus from the standpoint of power generation the objective of a reservoir operation is to store the snow melt run-off in the spring and early summer for release from storage in fall and winter when stream flows are lower and demand is higher.
The major migration of salmon and steelhead, both upstream and downstream, occurs during the spring and summer. To improve juvenile fish survival, changes have been made in the operation of the operation of the run-off river projects and at upstream storage reservoirs. All major dams and reservoirs in the Columbia River system are operated in co-ordination with one another to maximize the benefits provided by storage reservoirs.
The Pacific northwest has two principal flood seasons. November through March is the rain produced flood period. These floods occur most frequently on streams west of the Cascade Mountains. May through July is snow melt period, east of the Cascades. Snow melt floods dominate the run-off pattern in the Columbia basin. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendment moved by my colleague from Thunder Bay-Atikokan. I am very happy he moved the amendment so that I could speak again, also because I goofed in composing my motion when I forgot a crucial item, except that we were all under deadlines to file our motions.
After 25 years I will begin by saying that this may well be the last time in 25 years I have to speak in this Chamber and I do not know whether to die laughing or crying, but I will get into that a little later.
First, I want to talk about something dear to my heart and to many other members of the House from all sides. I want to talk about what has happened to our rail passenger system and service over the last number of years.
This country was world famous, recognized all over the world for the kind of transcontinental passenger train service that we had on both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. It has been marred by the fact that a private rail corporation and a public rail corporation decided they could not make any or enough money out of rail passengers so they chose to get out of the business and to hell with the country.
The government of that day was saddled with establishing VIA Rail. Thank goodness it did. The trouble is, VIA has been treated as an orphan by both a Liberal government and then a Conservative government ever since. It is still making do, surprisingly well, with equipment that is 30, 40 and 50 years of age. If I may put it in the vernacular of those who were on the railway in my days on the railway, it is a hell of a way to run a railway.
May 28, 1993

In retrospect it might have been better if the government of the day had decided to get out completely instead of doing it with these half-hearted measures. Imagine a modern railway in this century and the next operating on equipment 40 and 50 years of age. VIA has had to spend tens of millions of dollars refurbishing these old cars. It was finally allowed to buy some new locomotives. The old ones were at the point where they could not have pulled a push car.
Air Canada was the successor to CPR as an instrument of unifying this country and tying it together geographically. It did several things. First, it was privatized. The people of Canada put up all the money. CPR refused to come into the formation of Trans-Canada Airlines in 1935 and 1936. CPR said no. C.D. Howe, bless his dear departed soul, said: "To hell with you, we will start one up without you". We started up a national airline, Trans-Canada, CN and the government. The taxpayers put up the money. The taxpayers have been trying to get their money back ever since in terms of service on a true national Canadian airline.
The same thing applies to the rail system. The taxpayers of Canada paid for CPR, lock, stock and barrel from 1885 on. We gave them 25 million acres of land and it made a bundle out of that. It still owns property in downtown areas of every city in Canada and it has been, is now and will in the future make a bundle from the land the people of Canada gave it in return for building a railroad. That 25 million acres also included the mineral rights. Those mineral rights did not amount to much in the Atlantic provinces on the land given to CPR. It was a different story out west. CP has been making money in the four western provinces ever since then. It has been making a bundle. What did CP do? It proceeded to get out of the business. CPR signed a contract in 1885 that forever and a day, as the native people would say, as long as water runs down hill and grass grows green, it would run a railroad, freight and passenger service.
The dictates of the marketplace, the free enterprise system, globalization and all this nonsense has meant that in business terms CP had no other choice but to go back on the deal, double-cross and betray us and we end up with VIA Rail. VIA Rail is still operating with no

legislative mandate. It has operated on a $1 item in the estimates since the day it started-a $1 item.
We have been pleading as has VIA Rail. I met with President Ron Wallace a few weeks ago. The first requirement he has to have to succeed as a rail passenger corporation is a legislated mandate that outlines its responsibilities: what it can and cannot do. They still do not have legislation that sets up a national rail passenger corporation. That is ridiculous.

Believe it or not I even want to pay tribute to my favourite enemy, the CPR. They will have a heart attack when they hear this, if they do. My grandfather, my father and I worked for the CPR. There are relatively the same feelings in western Canada about the CPR.
There is the story of a farmer. The CPR killed his prize bull he had bought at the Regina Winter Fair. He had nothing but grief all the years he farmed and homesteaded out there. He would ship a can of cream and it would come back sour on its return. There would be no cheque. He would ship a crate of eggs and they would come back mostly broken on their return. It was nothing but a running battle with the CPR. A locomotive started a fire and his crop was burned. He got used to things like that. He went through all those years with the CPR.
Then one day a terrible storm hit. It rained. It flooded. The Lord sent everything down from the heavens that could be sent down. There were tornadoes and a mild earthquake. Everything occurred on this little farm in Saskatchewan. There were grasshoppers, here was hail and lightning, the whole thing, everything the Lord could send.
This farmer was enraged. He went outdoors, leaned back, stared to the heavens, held up his fists and said: "Lord, God damn the CPR". Sir, I hope you will pardon my language but I had to tell that prairie CPR story.
I appreciate, Sir, you allowing me to abuse my time allotment by more than a couple of minutes. I am grateful for that. I will get you a good line in my book if and when it ever gets printed so that you will buy extra copies.
I thank my colleagues for a wonderful time even when I was mad at them in spades. I am going to recall all the battles we have been in.
I will close by saying that in 25 years in this place I have never said it personally and I have never taken it personally. That must always be the underlying principle of every member who sits in this place. We can fight and argue about anything and everything, but it is never meant or said personally. It is never taken that way. In that way this Parliament will grow as will this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am inspired to respond to the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden, based on his last comment when he said that sometimes in this House he would get mad at you.
During the couple of years when I was Minister of Transport there was a period where I could expect when coming to the House of Commons I would have the hon. member mad at me. He will recall with fondness, as I recall with some regret, a bill called changing the Crow rate or the Western Grain Transportation Authority, where we spent about nine months together in this House day after day going after amendment after amendment. There was no more tenacious and knowledgeable critic of western rail transportation than the hon. member.
While he is in a confessional mood of his views of the House, I will also make a small confession. As much as the role one has to play in a ministerial post provides some disdain of opposition critics, I listened very carefully to the hon. member because I knew that when he was talking he knew what he was talking about.
I simply want to say that over the years he has demonstrated an incredible commitment to the basic principle of Canadian transportation as being the lifeblood of this country. I do not think in my 14 years or 15 years in the House, that anybody in this Chamber has
May 28, 1993

ever understood quite as well as the hon. member has, just how vital it is to maintain in this unique piece of geography of ours, that goes east and west not north and south we hope, the sense that you need good rail transportation, good air transportation and good people transportation.
It is no accident he comes from that part of the country, in the centre of the central plains where transportation is its life-blood, that he was able to bring to members of this House and to all Canadians, a very profound and important understanding of just how critical a part of public policy it was that we maintain a system of effective transportation that would move our grain, our potash, and our minerals and our people.
It is probably symbolic that in his last resolution in this House, as he says, that he comes back in some ways to-I do not know if it is his first love, because I am sure there are a few he has not told us about-one of his great loves and that is the system of VIA Rail and the need to maintain in this country a system of moving people in the regions. Especially in western Canada, we know how vital it is that we have a way of moving people from the towns and the communities by rail for those who cannot afford aeroplanes or those who find the great distances hard to accommodate. It is a resolution that I hope this House will pay some real attention to, not just because it is the hon. member, but because it simply makes a very effective presentation.
I can say, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues, that we have always respected the knowledge and commitment of the hon. member from Regina. I can say in a very personal way, having dealt with him in hand to hand combat across this House in the very vital period, that he really was one of the great builders of the transportation systems in this country. On behalf of our caucus, I certainly wish him well and good health.
